in writing. - (nl) during the first debate on the authorisation of long rigid buses on 3 october 2000, i said that it would be suitable for areas with low population density, where roads are wide and straight. in pedestrianised urban areas and on small, winding suburban roads, they can be a hazard to cyclists and pedestrians. in addition, without a second rear axle, they can be overloading on soft ground, as in the peat areas of the netherlands, and thus destroy the road surface. it is therefore perfectly justifiable that a number of eu member states only allow buses up to 12 metres in length. if these countries are forced to allow buses of 15 metres in length, they will have to put up additional signs of prohibition on their territory wherever necessary. these buses will have access to the country, but will not be able to operate in practice in many places. such buses are obviously more economical in terms of production and operation, and they will also consume less fuel per passenger. in the end, it appears that this is primarily a question of cost reduction, at the expense of safety. this was a principle reason for me at the time to reject the proposals and it remains so today. the council's proposal to authorize buses that do not meet the requirements of the directive until 2020, rather than 2009, will also not receive my assent.
in writing. - (nl) in every occupational sector where the activity is not linked to a specific location, it is noted that some employers try to have the work done by people from other states for less pay. this can be done by outsourcing financial administration in india, or by outsourcing clothing to the philippines, or by having lorries driven by bulgarian or lithuanian drivers in western europe. free competition provides great advantages to firms with the lowest possible costs and the highest possible profits. they take market share at the expense of other companies, even if it is at the expense of jobs, the environment or animal welfare. as long as the authorities do not stop this, the worst companies have the best chance of survival. in the transport of goods, this leads to the use of a driver recruited in the east, outside the territory of a member state, who is paid in black. not only is the pay unacceptable, but so are the working conditions. the introduction of a driver attestation with the driver's licence and social security numbers of the person concerned was delayed too long. i can agree that this applies to non-eu drivers initially, but as of 2004 their countries of origin may be part of the eu. effective control will then require that the certificate is also required for drivers of lorries resident in the eu.

in writing. - (nl) public procurement has long been regarded as a miracle cure. they are an alternative to nepotism, in other words, the awarding of contracts by contracting authorities to entrepreneurs allied to politicians or high-ranking civil servants; on the other hand, they also aim to put an end to the supply of goods and services by undertakings owned by the public authorities themselves and, consequently, to give private undertakings access to new markets. i can approve the first reason but not the second. it makes governments dependent on business. it has recently emerged in the netherlands that construction companies are in dispute with each other about the price that the public authorities should pay for the award of contracts. in this way, the companies decided among themselves who would be the next customer. it is a de facto monopoly. although this is punishable, it is extremely difficult to prevent such a process in practice. i think it is positive that the rapporteur's proposals would free contracting authorities in the context of relatively small contracts from the costly and confusing obligation to use the european public procurement procedure, that employment could be guaranteed for disadvantaged groups, that environmental criteria would be better taken into account and that those who have been convicted of financial misconduct could be excluded from the tenders. i approve of these improvements, but not the whole procurement procedure.
in writing. - (nl) the profession of chauffeur has been practised for many years without having undergone very long training. since some drivers had indeed completed a full cycle of schooling, this training was not considered to be of value for the work to be done. this made the job attractive to all those who had difficulty in obtaining an education and who, from a very young age, could earn an income in an activity in which they enjoyed a relative autonomy. many who have the necessary licence to drive lorries or buses may therefore be unhappy if stricter requirements are imposed on their work. they are exempted from basic training to avoid becoming unemployed and are only required to undergo five years of continuing training. the number of training hours to be required - a minimum of 210 hours and a maximum of 630 hours - is lower than is already required in some member states. these member states must now accept that drivers from other countries with only limited training may be employed in their territory. the contribution to improved road safety, fuel economy, good public relations, active language skills and improved working conditions is therefore very limited. for these reasons, i consider this proposal to be a first step which should be followed by a series of others in the longer term.
- (nl) fifty years ago, space navigation was considered a major step forward. not only by readers of novels about supposed humanoids inhabiting other planets, but also and especially from the point of view of the competition between the two most powerful nations on earth. all that remains of this space conquest is a museum in moscow, filled with space rockets and mannequins, as well as images from the films brought back by the americans who walked on the moon in 1969. we have not been to the moon for a long time, and the next space exploration can be done from the earth with ever more sophisticated telescopes. the only major space project europe is preparing is a satellite system for global navigation and location, which is supposed to compete globally with the us system already in operation. i already said on 3 october 2001, when we voted on the langenhagen report, that i found this project, which is extremely expensive, quite superfluous. i can understand why my colleague, mr alyssandrakis, finds such projects exciting because they correspond to his scientific expertise in this field. however, i consider it to be primarily a costly prestige project from which most citizens in europe and our environment will not benefit. this is at most in the military interest, certainly if the anti-militarist considerations contained in the report are dismissed in the vote. for these reasons, i reject this proposal.

- madam president, criminal law is closely linked to the national identity of the member states. national history and culture have colored the penal laws in various ways. this is precisely why we see great differences between the criminal laws of the european union. the open european area and the growth of international crime have made it clear that cooperation in this area is necessary if the union is to remain an area of security and justice. the tampere european council did not endorse the principle of mutual recognition in criminal matters within the european union for nothing. this proposal is a start on the implementation of the principle of mutual recognition. i think it is a good initiative on the part of the united kingdom, france and sweden to start on this fairly clear ground with mutual recognition in criminal matters. the proposal is quite simple in its design. in principle, the principle of double criminality applies, i.e. to the requesting member state and the executing member state. the absence of such a requirement shall be a reason for non-enforcement of the sanction by the executing member state. the simplicity of the proposal itself could make it work much better than the international conventions have done so far. many in this parliament would prefer a proposal for the harmonization of criminal law. they believe that harmonisation at european level will lead to greater confidence in the criminal law of other member states and in its application. i doubt this is right. trust cannot be imposed from above by harmonizing legislation. it is precisely where diversity is allowed to exist and even seen as an added value that mutual trust can emerge. and practical experience is often the best method of gaining or losing confidence. this is why mutual recognition is a very good instrument for cooperation in this sensitive area. and indeed, the need for mutual recognition will slow down cooperation in criminal matters in other areas. but if it is slow, it also means that there is clearly not enough trust. the attempt to force this through imposed harmonization could have a counter-effect. the amendments tabled by the cerdeira monterero report are largely practical improvements. i particularly support the rapporteur's proposal to use the contact points of the european judicial network and not to set up new contact points. this would unnecessarily complicate european legal cooperation. i disagree with amendment no 3. it adds the charter of fundamental rights of the eu as a framework for the review of union acts. however, the charter has the status of a political declaration and not of a legal framework for evaluation. the echr, on the other hand, which has been signed by all eu states and future member states, is legally enforceable. the suggestion that the texts are on the same level is wrong.

the rapporteur. - mr president, i shall try to get beyond the noise. the present report deals with a draft council framework decision which the commission has submitted to us. this is part of the creation of an area of freedom, security and justice, as we have also been promised in the treaties, especially since amsterdam, and for which a programme was also explicitly planned at later summits. but this is not a very far-reaching proposal. in this case, the common fight against crossborder crime is to be pursued, in particular by agreeing on the minimum maximum penalty to be laid down in the laws of the member states. in fact, the whole text has been written in such a way as to give it the best chance of being accepted by the council and, as such, it is little more than a major common denominator of what will be included in the law books of the member states.
- mr president, drug policy has often given rise to heated debates in the european parliament. extensive abuse then turned everything upside down, touching family, faith and authority. we're in a little quieter waters today. the european commission's proposal is limited to the legal aspects and we should be sober about that. as the commission rightly emphasizes in its proposal, the responsibility for combating illicit drug trafficking lies primarily with the member states. however, as it is often organised trade that extends to several countries, a framework decision addressing this cross-border trade can be a useful complement to national policies. what is missing from the commission's proposal, however, is a distinction between the different types of drugs and therefore a differentiated criminalization of the illegal drug trade. more and more countries in europe are distinguishing soft drugs from hard drugs on the basis of the health risks they pose, and there is also growing political support for policies based on fair information and prevention of health risks. on this basis, some member states have a tolerant policy towards soft drugs. the present framework decision is not intended to undermine this policy. as regards the penalties, a wide range of factors must be taken into account in order to arrive at an effective and proportionate penalty. unfortunately, the criteria for determining the seriousness of the fact, such as the volume of trade, the frequency and the nature of the means involved, are not included in the proposal. that is why my group, together with three other groups, has tabled an amendment to include such criteria. the cultural differences and the different prosecution policies of the member states, as well as the principle of subsidiarity, justify the restriction of this proposal to the organised and crossborder illegal drug trade. the vast majority of my group sees added value in this framework decision only if it is restricted.
- the rapporteur has just asked us to refrain from referring to legalization or not, or toleration or not, because that is not the issue here. i'm not so sure about that, though. illegal drug trafficking is just too general a term for me. mr oostlander is opposed to the dutch practice of tolerance and that is fine. i think it's a half-baked compromise myself. i myself would prefer to see the legalisation of soft drugs, soft drugs which are, after all, less harmful than the alcohol which also flows freely in this building. it is not only in the netherlands that soft drugs are tolerated. for reasons of public health, this policy is also being followed in other countries at local, regional and sometimes even national level. even if we make tough statements now, the practice will be different. let us therefore limit ourselves to a policy which we can implement, which is also a european task under the principle of subsidiarity and on which there is broad parliamentary and social agreement, namely tackling the lucrative, organised, crossborder drug trade. the rest of us can take on mr oostlander at national level, because the elections are coming up.
- the proposal for a directive on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the labelling, presentation and advertising of foodstuffs for sale to the ultimate consumer; it is merely a codification of the lowest common denominator of legislation in the member states. i am quite happy with the commission's cautious approach. criminal justice is a field strongly shaped by national culture and history. in my view, the main reason for this is that there is still reluctance to transfer powers to the european level. only where there are clearly cross-border problems does european regulation provide added value. this view seems to be shared by few in parliament. i am surprised that i am being overtaken on the right this time by my colleagues from the socialist and european regulation, namely the illegal drug trade. my colleagues want to add the words transnational and organised to the definition. it seems to me that these concepts are inherent in the drug trade the commission has already made a number of proposals to improve the commission's proposal. firstly, the strengthening of the ability to reap the profits of drug criminals. if we can get these people where it really hurts, which is in their wallets, then this will be much more effective than higher sentences. we should also not focus on the prosecution of addicts, but clearly focus on prevention. that is a good signal for europe to focus on with limited resources. but here our paths diverge. i am very pleased that, following a european trend towards a more realistic drug policy, a majority of the european liberal group will support all the amendments aimed at making a distinction between hard drugs and soft drugs, the non-prosecution of users as well as the amendments which will limit this proposal to cross-border, criminal drug trafficking. let us focus our limited resources on the big criminals and not on the small users. i would like to warn the ppe colleagues who speak of dangerous signals that this parliament would send out, of symbolism. we have no say in this matter. my group also questions two specific proposals from the commission. it is not wise to limit the minimum maximum sentence of five years to certain crimes and to apply it to all drug offences. we shall also support the amendment for a limitation. finally, we find the provision for informers who should receive a reduction in their sentences in exchange for information on drug gangs to be very far-reaching. this is a very sensitive subject in which the different member states have different traditions. to suddenly go about this in this way, so short of a turn, is going to take us a long way.
the rapporteur. − mr president, commissioners, the european union is the world's largest donor of emergency aid. european money is helping people affected by war or natural disasters in bangladesh, afghanistan, somalia and the balkans to get back on their feet. but too often, the direct aid is stopped and replaced by aid for the reconstruction and development of the affected area. a problem referred to in the literature as the grey zone. to illustrate, let us take an example from the school textbooks. after hurricane mitch left a trail of destruction across central america in 1998, the union responded swiftly with emergency aid. the commission then began work in 1999 on an action programme for the reconstruction of central america, and echo was to leave the region in march 2001. the action programme had good elements such as local participation, coordination with the member states and other donors, and decentralisation of powers to the managua delegation. in practice, however, the programme was far too slow. two years after the disaster, only a few projects had been approved. unfortunately, this example is the rule rather than the exception and is of course unacceptable from both a political and a humanitarian point of view. who will explain to the people of afghanistan that we cannot keep our promise of help because of our own inability to respond quickly and flexibly after the emergency phase? the question is what measures the commission is taking to avoid the grey area problem in the reconstruction of afghanistan. the commission and the organisations concerned in the field have been extensively consulted in the preparation of this report. the commission recognizes the problem of the grey area, but at the same time its evaluation which we are discussing today remains too vague and too theoretical. that is why my report, based in part on the conference with the ngos concerned and intensive discussions with your civil service, makes a number of concrete proposals to the commission. the commission notes that inflexible and bureaucratic procedures are one of the key problems. as a solution, the commission proposes to draw up annexes to the country strategy notes which should allow for a rapid and flexible response in a crisis situation. i support this proposal, but only if the addenda are adopted within two months. has the commission already established new, simplified, rapid and flexible procedures for the approval and adaptation of the annexes? otherwise, the proposal for these crisis documents will remain a dead letter. i would also like to point out, as rapporteur, the enormous importance of coordination and cooperation, not only between the commission services but also with the member states, international donors, local partners and ngos. my discussions with the commission have clearly shown the need for a flexible instrument for reconstruction and rehabilitation so that this grey area can be tackled. the existing rehabilitation regulation is too limited. projects in areas such as safety and good governance are outside the scope of the regulation and there is little money available. it is clear that the total amount of some eur 50 million for asia, for example, is far below the need in afghanistan. i therefore propose that the existing rehabilitation regulation be revised so that in the post-crisis phase it can be flexible enough to respond to the real needs of the population in an affected area. in order to ensure sufficient funds, money must be released quickly from the existing unused budget and reserves through a trigger mechanism at the time of a crisis. how does the commission intend to translate my plan into concrete proposals? the problem of the grey area between emergency and rehabilitation is well known. we must no longer accept that people who are directly affected by war or natural disasters in their daily lives are left out of the picture by our inability to respond quickly, flexibly and in a coordinated way to the local situation. as europe's largest donor of emergency aid worldwide, we must also close the gap with sustainable development in crisis areas. this would be a major contribution to security and stability in conflict regions in asia, latin america and africa. that is perhaps a wiser investment than the commitment of large sums for defence equipment such as the f16s, although i know that the commission is not going to discuss that. as your rapporteur, i will therefore continue to monitor closely how the commission and the member states tackle this problem in the near future. i expect a lot from the commitments made so far, but i am very much looking forward to the commission's concrete response.
- the commission is good at analysis, but often lacks the administrative capacity to actually implement policy conclusions. the internal organisation is still too hierarchical, bureaucratic and centralised, and the member states give the commission too few resources and too little policy space to operate effectively. these structural deficiencies therefore prevent the solution of the grey area problem. the transition from emergency aid to reconstruction and development requires flexibility in decision-making. the commission has also been asked to provide a report on the implementation of the new rules on the protection of the environment. the first requirement is, of course, an optimal prevention policy in the face of natural disasters and violent conflicts. everything possible must be done before a crisis breaks out. the readiness must be optimal, plans must be ready, coordination links must be agreed and the implementing partners must be known as much as possible. detailed and flexible emergency plans should be part of the country programmes. echo should focus on emergency relief, but it seems highly desirable that it also incorporate expertise in the field of reconstruction in its staff to facilitate a smoother transition. the control of implementation must be shifted from ex ante to ex post. internal coordination can only be successful if a multidisciplinary team is put to work at an early stage. when can we expect concrete proposals from the commission on simplified policy procedures? the report by mr van den berg makes excellent suggestions. the entire donor community is responsible for improvement. the grey area problem is another reason for urgency in the internal reorganization of the commission. it is high time that the fine analyses were translated into even more fine policy actions.

in writing. - (nl) if the measures for residents and non-european visitors had not been prepared before 11 september 2001, they would probably have remained unfinished for a long time, given the new phobia of terrorism and insecurity. it is high time that we put an end to the last vestiges of legal rejection inflicted on a large part of our population. this discrimination affects people who were mainly attracted during the 1960s as "immigrant workers" from turkey or morocco to perform the most unrewarding and poorly paid tasks. the six member states which then made up the european communities did not initially take account of their permanent establishment. forty years later, many of those of the first generation of immigrants still do not have the nationality of the country in which they reside. these people have known no european unity for years. unlike nationals of other member states, they had to continue to meet visa requirements in all member states crossed to go on holiday in their country of origin. the fact that they are now granted more equal rights is unfortunately not due to the indignation aroused by the lack of respect shown to them but rather the result of the desire to build a single european superstate and to demonstrate that the old national borders have largely lost their usefulness.

in writing. - (nl) for a long time, the search for ever faster vehicles has been on, both for the transport of goods and for the transport of passengers. the speed limit was considered a temporary and undesirable feature of a technique which was still imperfect. any voluntary attempt to return to any form of speed limitation was seen as an infringement of the individual freedom of the motorist or as an obstacle to a favorable turnover for transport companies. the increasing number of road accidents is changing our minds. however, the introduction of devices for an increasingly large proportion of traffic is only one part of the solution. if we impose speed limitation without adequately limiting the legal speed, it is more like a hidden subsidy to companies that can conquer a new market. this is comparable to the agreement with the automotive industry, which provides headlamps that automatically turn on when the vehicle starts, after which the driver must switch them off again in order to comply with national legal provisions or safety requirements. the rapporteur unfortunately limits the proposal to commercial cars, extends the transition periods and increases part of the maximum speed for motor vehicles of category n2 to 110 km. speed limiters only make sense if they are designed to enforce a serious legal speed limit, and unfortunately there is still no such limit.

in writing. - (nl) a large part of the powers ceded by the national parliaments for the sake of european unification have not returned to the european parliament but to the national governments. the existence of the european union has thus strengthened the power of ministers and secretaries of state. the way in which they conclude agreements between themselves in the council cannot be controlled by either the european parliament or the national parliaments. if a decision is taken that is contrary to national public opinion, they can always say that they wanted to do the right thing but that neighbours unfortunately prevented them from doing so. the ministers of the neighbouring countries say the same. this intergovernmental version of the decision-making process is no longer a guarantee that the different wishes of the member states are taken into account. i therefore advocate an interparliamentary rather than an intergovernmental version of the decisionmaking process. the european commission makes proposals, the european parliament decides on first reading and the national parliaments then each deliberate separately on the applicability of these decisions in their country. in this model, the council no longer has any independent decision-making function. unfortunately, mr napolitano's proposals do not go that far, but they do, and rightly so, strengthen the role of parliaments at different levels in relation to the leaders.
in writing. - (nl) as long as the structural funds exist in their present form, there will continue to be tensions between the regional and the european sides. from a regional point of view, this is own funds to which we are entitled and which we must be able to spend independently as freely as possible. from the european point of view, it is european money, made available under strict conditions for use in regions or cities, and which must be claimed if deadlines are exceeded or if the intended destination is missed. it is possible to reconcile these conflicting desires only through a lot of prior consultation and a lot of control. this means that there are high costs and a lot of bureaucracy involved in allocating these funds. it is probably preferable for europe to limit itself to redistributing funds freely usable for investment in regions lagging behind, suffering from a crisis or economically unfavourable geographical situation, and to interfere with little or no involvement in the use made of them. such a change would make it possible to use european civil servants for other tasks that still leave much to be desired and to put an end to the unnecessary pumping of money from rich member states to the same rich member states. there will indeed be fewer propaganda signs with a european flag, but it is still much more effective.

in writing. - (nl) in march 2000, the lisbon summit took a decision characterised by a lack of foresight. the justified desire to secure livelihoods for all has not translated into a more equitable distribution of existing work based on a general reduction in working time, early retirement and the strengthening of public services, but has given rise to the desire to further strengthen economic growth for private enterprises. as a result of this growth and competition with the other two major economic powers, existing public services in the field of public transport, energy supply, post and telecommunications are also likely to fall into the hands of large international groups. this is a disastrous course because it subjects our peoples to competition and we will find ourselves in the midst of a serious economic crisis if europe ever loses this competition. privatizations also weaken the power of our democratically elected members of parliament and encourage savings in labour costs. the 'social europe' advocated by some supporters of the lisbon decisions is thus absent, since the 'europe of capital' is the only one to emerge. the bullmann report unfortunately follows this wrong path, confusing 'social' with 'capital', but it does not go far enough for the right. that is why i voted against.
in writing. -{nl) in a democratic state, political and ethnic minorities also have rights. this is still not the case in turkey. everyone has to adapt to the dominant language and culture, and to join the majority opinion about the lack of rights of ethnic minorities in this country. anyone who speaks another language, raises another flag or creates a party that is especially successful in a certain part of the country is accused of separatism, while the inhabitants of areas where a minority is the majority suffer under the yoke of destruction and oppression. the ethnic massacre of armenians in 1915 is still not recognized, perhaps because of the desire to preserve the possibility of its repetition. while the turkish state recognizes other new states in europe, such as bosnia-herzegovina, lithuania and slovakia, it is extremely fearful of the modest demands for autonomy and cultural rights of a very large minority on its own territory. for many years there have been systematic attempts to exclude kurdish members of the turkish parliament by imposing a 10% electoral threshold and banning political parties. it is therefore essential that a majority in the european parliament make it clear to turkey that it will never have a place in the european union as long as ethnic inequalities and oppression persist.

by regional competition authorities - of far too great concentrations of power. these rules include protection and support for weaker regions and the drastic opening up of richer markets to developing countries. the protection of the strongest through a system of social control over transnational enterprises is not in this context, although the latter would be a good thing. it is not the unilateral action of transnational corporations or major powers such as the united states, nor is it the unilateral concentration on a new arms race at the expense of public services such as education and health care. nor does it include the failure to meet the pledge to halve poverty by 2015. what does fit in is fair trade with rules, democratic control of global rules and social and good behaviour of transnational companies. respect for human values and societies over commercial interests. it is a modern and open world, and it is based on mutual interest and respect for each other's differences, on the basis of a commonly recognised legal order. and that right includes the right to a chance to shape your own life. and then, mr president, we are back to monterrey. the scandal of the spanish presidency's failure to translate the concrete agreements reached by our ministers for development cooperation last week into an agreement to supplement 0.7% of gdp with concrete steps. it is unacceptable to follow the united states, which puts money and values first, and then close the poverty gap. we demand broad security, worldwide, and the fulfillment of the promise to send all girls and boys to school healthy and fed by 2015. we, the socialists in the european parliament, demand that the spanish presidency keep its promise. this is our contribution to world peace and we want to translate the lessons of porto alegre and new york into a new role for europe in this world.

and the conditions under which it is done - lies with the member states. that's a good thing too. the situation in the various member states varies considerably. in order to ensure adequate service provision for each member state and region, it is appropriate for member states to apply a licensing system, including the possibility of performance criteria. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the services provided by the regions are adequate. a thorough, broad evaluation will have to be made to determine this. on the basis of that evaluation, this discussion will have to be continued at a later stage. in conclusion, mr president, i believe that the present common position, including the amendment by the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, can be described as a balanced position on the development of the postal services market. our delegation will therefore support it.

in writing. -{nl) in the past we had a system of electricity production and distribution organised at the municipal or provincial level and placed under the responsibility of the popular representation of the territory in question. today we are moving towards a system where production and distribution will be carried out by international groups without any democratic influence. the california blackouts and the enron bankruptcy have already made us fully aware of the disadvantages of such a system. in fact, some of the negative consequences are already visible in europe. the dutch distribution companies, which until recently were owned by the municipalities and provinces, have invested heavily in the production of clean electricity. since this type of production is now too expensive, these companies use the crossborder connection network to import dirty electricity produced with coal, lignite or nuclear energy. while this interconnection network was built to enable mutual aid in the event of disaster or to cope with spikes in consumption, its capacity is now being diverted to the benefit of international trade. i therefore reject the content of the mombaur report on crossborder trade in electricity, even though the proposals of mr turmes and mr rapkay are in favour of accounting for greenhouse gases and nuclear waste, stimulating windmills and cogeneration and protecting consumers. these objectives will ultimately prove irreconcilable and i reject this proposal.

the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the protection of the environment from harmful substances. the subject is exciting. exciting, because the legal system chosen is beautiful, but it will also provide a great deal of food for european legal scholars for years to come. the commission, parliament and the council fully share the view that member states should have the possibility of imposing criminal sanctions as an enforcement instrument for european environmental legislation. the way in which such a system of criminal sanctions for serious environmental offences should be formulated and initiated and the question of who should be allowed to take part in the decision-making process, divides us. with the rapporteur, mr di lello, from the committee on civil liberties, i am taking the european commission's side here and i am going for a directive on environmental crime under the first pillar. the council opted for the danish proposal for measures under the third pillar. the members of the committee on civil liberties rightly reject this. what binds the council, parliament and the commission is that we all want to follow up the very explicit request of the tampere european council in october 1999 for common definitions, penalties and penalties targeting a limited number of sectors of particular importance, but mentioning environmental crime in particular. since the choice of the legal basis in the first pillar raises questions for the council - and, as i have just heard, for some of my colleagues in the group - i shall make a few clarifying remarks, which i hope will also convince doubters. i do so on the basis of a number of points. why do we go for the first pillar, and i advise you to go for the first pillar? first of all: the council, with the danish proposal, is based on article 31 preamble and letter (e) of the eu treaty, which gives the power to act jointly in the field of judicial cooperation in criminal matters and which provides for the gradual adoption of measures establishing minimum rules on the constituent elements of criminal offences and on penalties in the field of organised crime, terrorism and drug trafficking. this provision is contained in title vi. however, under article 29 of the eu treaty, the provisions of that title apply, and i quote, 'without prejudice to the powers of the european community'. but article 47 of the eu treaty also states that the eu treaty does not affect the treaties establishing the european communities. that means, mr president, that criminal law is not the exclusive domain of the european union. the case law of the european court of justice, to which i also refer in the report, confirms that the eu treaty cannot impose any obstacles. a second point: the question which arises next, since there are no general obstacles to criminal proceedings under the ec treaty, is: what can, what is the ec allowed to do specifically? if we look at article 280 (4) of the ec treaty, which is in line with article 5 which lays down the principle of subsidiarity, i would observe that in the area of environmental criminal law too care must be taken that ec legislation does not disturb the organisation of national criminal law. a third point: it is therefore crucial that this directive does not deal with specific provisions on criminal law, but that criminal law is used to make environmental policy effective. the use of criminal law is in many areas an important factor in the enforcement of the rules, and, thus, while respecting that subsidiarity, a certain degree of coordination of the use of criminal law enforcement can be useful for the full implementation of community provisions. fourthly: the proposal on environmental crime is based on article 175 (1) of the ec treaty, which provides that the council, acting in accordance with the co-decision procedure laid down in article 251, shall take all measures necessary to achieve the environmental objective set out in article 174, provided that subsidiarity does not prevent this. a fifth point: the proposal for a directive is in line with environmental directives and regulations adopted on the basis of article 175 (1) and adds only a criminal aspect to that legislation. the existing line is thus extended, with the directive requiring member states to provide for criminal sanctions for activities which cause significant damage to the environment. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect, and i am sure that the commission will be able to support them. i have left article 1 of the directive, which aims to establish minimum standards for criminal offences, unchanged. the member states are thus free to determine the level of the penalty. in article 2 i have also included in the definitions the term 'incitement to environmental action', which i have based on the so-called danish proposal. thirdly, i have included the offences now listed in the annex under article 3, with two minor amendments. i strongly reject amendment no 22, because i do not think there is a legal basis for it. the fourth point: in article 4, i clarify the concept of 'framework'. instead of having the member states decide on the penalties, it is better to use the concept of criminal sanctions. i am amending amendment no 25 because subsidiarity is also important here. we can only invite the member states to introduce measures such as confiscation if this element is also very specifically mentioned in their own legal systems. mr president, this directive is like dancing on a silk string. we as the european parliament must be very precise, because i assume that the european court of justice will be examining this and we may be going there with the help of the european commission. finally, i would like to thank my colleagues, not only those in the committee on the environment and the rapporteur for the committee on civil liberties, but also the colleagues in the legal affairs committee and all the shadow rapporteurs. we have worked together in a united spirit, mr president, and although the contribution may seem very technical at the moment, there is a lot of politics behind it, which is of interest not only to the commission but certainly also to the european parliament. we serve a good cause: the protection of the environment.
the criminal law in the member states on environmental offences is still a matter of debate. the deliberate pollution of our environment cannot be adequately combated by this. one of the reasons is that the european directives are not being implemented, respected and enforced. experience has shown that the current penalties for breaches of european and national environmental legislation are not sufficient, to say the least. it seems that only criminal sanctions are sufficient deterrents to ensure compliance with environmental legislation. the european environmental legislation is not without reason, since we are dealing with transboundary effects in air pollution and water pollution, among other things. in addition, there are many negative consequences of transporting waste to places where there is no environmentally responsible treatment. it also has the potential to disrupt the internal market. these reasons lead me to support an international approach to environmental crime. i believe that the present directive is an appropriate and effective means of doing so. the oomen-ruijten report provides convincing evidence of this. the question remains whether we need a framework decision from the council for this. finally, mr president, i shall vote for the directive but i am inclined to vote against the draft framework decision unless commissioner vitorino can convince me that the framework decision is absolutely necessary for the directive to enter into force.

- mr president, the european union's common foreign and security policy is slowly taking shape. good intentions are being translated into increasingly concrete actions and the development of the rapid intervention force is progressing steadily. the first deployment of these could hopefully take place in macedonia. nevertheless, even the assembly of a force of some 2000 troops remains a difficult task, for which the european union cannot yet do without nato, and this creates the necessary problems. cooperation with nato is in itself a good thing, because it allows us to be operational more quickly, but it is also a complicating factor, as the talks with turkey have shown. in the longer term, the european union must strive for full autonomy in the deployment of the rapid intervention force. the development of the still lacking military capacity is therefore urgent. the european union is not nato and nato is not the united nations. we can't switch roles. the european union does not seek to be an organisation for collective defence. it is not a military superpower and it is a multilateral approach to international problems through the un and other international organisations. recently, striking differences have emerged between the european union and the united states. these are largely the result of differing views on safety. the common foreign and security policy is in fact the expression of the history of europe over the last 100 years. the cooperation model is the most important. the military instrument is much less emphasized than in the united states, and this is not only because of the absence of a military superpower status. we have recognised the relative value of the instrument and therefore place much more emphasis on the use of civilian means such as diplomacy and economic cooperation. it is not for nothing that conflict prevention and conflict resolution have become an important part of our policy. the enlargement of the european union and the balkans are examples of this. but it also explains the renewed focus on poverty reduction, and not just because of 9/11. such a policy is multilateral in nature and it also explains why we react with horror to sharon's military approach. we know from our own painful experience that this only adds to the problems. the united states, in many cases, sees things differently. the possession of military power and its possible use are paramount. if necessary, we'll do it alone, you hear them say. one example is the us position on arms control, and another example is the threatening language towards iraq. we are of course in favour of stopping the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, starting with iraq. we need the united nations and the eu to help us make this policy possible. we certainly cannot rule out coercion, but violence is not the first thing to be obvious. there has been a kind of unnatural division of labour between the european union and the united states. they use their military superiority and thus often determine policy, while the european union often reverses the damage; at least, it often seems that way. that is unsustainable in the long run. we believe that civilian power is more important than military power and that this should be the core of the transatlantic dialogue.

in writing. - (nl) there is a conflict of interest between industrial enterprises and all the others. consumers and the environment would like products to be made that are sustainable, with every part of the product being reusable at the end of its life. industry, on the other hand, tends to aim for the most competitive selling prices possible and, subsequently, for the lowest possible possible possible possible costs. it is also in the interest of the commission to pass on the problems to others, in particular the public authorities, whose task it is to find solutions with taxpayers' money. industry has tried to weaken the proposals in its favour. i, too, have been approached with what seemed like reasonable arguments. environmental fanatics would like expensive and unrealistic solutions, whereas environmental objectives could be achieved without constraint. they may be right in some cases. however, to give in to these arguments would be to open the door to less well-intentioned competitors who, without assuming their responsibilities and thus offering lower prices, are eager to conquer and expand markets. for these reasons, it is good that we adopt regulations on the recycling of 'abandoned' products from companies that no longer exist, or 'historic' waste from unknown producers, or waste produced before the directive comes into force. the exceptions for small enterprises are not justified, especially for military equipment. unfortunately, the christian-democratic group is once again counting on these 314 votes to secure its satisfaction.
in writing. - (nl) my group voted against the opinion on the community patent because it rejected the eldr group's proposals on three fundamental points. the european market requires a uniform and economically affordable patent system. the debate on the language regime has unfortunately shown that political sentiment has prevailed over practical arguments. translation costs disproportionately increase the cost of patents and therefore make them too expensive for european companies, the end users. that is why my group is in favour of a restricted language regime and cannot approve the 'alicante' regime, which provides for five languages (amendments 31 and 32). in addition, the uniform application of the regulation is essential. that is why my group has proposed that the community intellectual property court should be the central authority for dealing with patent disputes, with appeals being the responsibility of the court of justice (amendments nos 26 and 29). finally, my liberal colleagues and i prefer the establishment of an autonomous community system to accession to the munich convention. the commission has also proposed that the council should be able to adopt a decision on the basis of the opinion of the european parliament.
in writing. - (nl) the existence of patents prevents the free use of any discovery which seems to have already been made by someone else. on the one hand, it is good that intellectual property is protected against opportunists eager to profit from the efforts of others over many years. on the other hand, patents prevent third world countries from producing medicines to combat widespread tropical diseases and allow the heirs of certain inventors to levy a kind of tax on genetically modified plants or animals that are marketed. for countries with a technological and economic backlog, the best way to catch up is to deny the existence of patent rights. for 40 years there has been talk of setting up, alongside national patent systems, a world patent in the making and the existence of a european patent office which is not subordinate to the eu, a community patent, a principle still disputed within the council. in the end, this proposal is all about the use of languages, a system where english, french, german, spanish and italian would be privileged over the other official languages of the eu member states, including the 22 million dutch and 40 million polish speakers. as this proposal is not mature enough for us to take a decision, i will not support it.

report drawn up on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy. - mr president, in the 1960s and 1970s asbestos was seen as a miracle drug in construction, in industry and as a road surfacing material. by now many victims who have inhaled asbestos dust have died from it. long after the devastating effects of asbestos were known, the use of this relatively inexpensive material continued in various lands. even if its use ends by 2005, we will still have a long negative legacy. in the next 30 years, half a million people in western europe alone will be disabled and die prematurely, since the disease often does not manifest itself until long after infection. the claim for grief-money, compensation, invalidity and survivor's pensions is justified. asbestos is present in buildings, equipment and vehicles in countless places and must be removed in an expert manner. the problem is even greater in the eastern states which are seeking to join the european union, partly because many houses in the countryside are built with roofs and facades made entirely of russian-origin asbestos. the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection has tabled 15 additional amendments to focus on people who have never worked with asbestos themselves but who may be exposed to it, such as family members, residents of dwellings containing in writing. - (nl) thanks to the d66 delegation, the oostlander report on drug trafficking has been amended so that its scope now covers only the large-scale, crossborder and organised trafficking. the netherlands' policy on soft drugs is therefore not affected. however, d66 abstained in the final vote on the report. the reason for this is that amendments nos 5 and 14 have been adopted by parliament. the amendments require member states to use the proceeds of drug seizures for drug addiction programmes. as sympathetic as this objective is, we find it wrong in principle to make aid programmes financially dependent on the results of the fight against crime. our preference therefore remains for the dutch method, whereby fines and profits from seized products are added to the regular resources which finance the aid programmes. these amendments are contrary to the principle of subsidiarity. despite the considerable improvements we have made, we have therefore had to abstain on this report.
in writing. - (nl) my party, the dutch socialist party, is in favour of a high level of protection of man and the environment and is prepared to accept a high level of fiscal pressure to this end. the quality of public services in the fields of education, health, public transport and environmental protection comes at a price and cannot be undermined by austerity measures. on the other hand, we have no sympathy for the diversion of funds to military objectives, uncontrolled economic growth and the giving of gifts to profit-seeking businesses. the use of taxes by a body close to the citizens, on which they have the greatest influence, generally offers a much better quality and is more in line with the democratic will of the voters than the management of the same funds by an uncontrollable body so far removed from most citizens. we therefore believe that it is not self-evident that the european union should be given as much money as possible. the movement of structural funds between the richest member states, the current agricultural policy, which is geared towards large farms, and the increasingly close interplay with nato policy do not seem to us to be good uses of these funds. on the other hand, we support solidarity with the poorest regions, development aid to the third world and greater respect for the environment. we therefore approve the distribution of surpluses between the existing community plans and their reimbursement to the member states.

the rapporteur. by 3 june, the council, commission and parliament should have fully implemented the european law on the transparency of public administration, i.e. the regulation on access to documents. for the european parliament, this means that the list of parliament documents which will be directly accessible through the register should be annexed to the rules of procedure of parliament. the attached annex shall require the agreement of a simple majority of the members; the debate on this will take place today and the vote tomorrow. the list presented is for the most part the result of a precise legal application of the regulation. a team led by the parliament's deputy secretary-general has drawn up the first list. the committee on constitutional affairs has a small number of documents attached to it, which are not required but desirable to be made public. i mention the working documents, recommendations and statements of the parliamentary delegations which were not on the original list the attendance lists of plenary and committee meetings which are, moreover, recorded in the minutes and are therefore also indirectly public and the list of members' staff. as rapporteur, i support these additions, some of which are also my own. as regards the publication of the list of staff, i believe that this should be in accordance with the decision of the office of 11 june 2001, which states that the members and staff themselves should be responsible for the information contained in the public list. i hope, mr president, that the whole list can be approved. however, restrictions which are not in accordance with the regulation cannot be accepted, because otherwise we will be ordered by the european court of justice to complete the list again and parliament will have blamed itself. with this list, the european parliament has fulfilled all its obligations in implementing the regulation. is everything all right with this? unfortunately, that is not yet the case. neither the european commission nor the council have, in our view, fulfilled all the conditions for the implementation of the regulation. the commission has not yet taken all the necessary steps, particularly in relation to documents from third parties, such as member states or external organisations. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european parliament is able to exercise its right of initiative in the matter of the internal market. that too will have to be arranged. in general, the disclosure of third party documents is still a major problem, because the commission and the council are more rigid than desirable in this respect. in fact, it is urgent that member states which do not yet have adequate legislation on the transparency of governance should themselves draw up such legislation as soon as possible. it would also remove the objections which some member states still express. it cannot be that the level of openness to citizens in one eu country is much higher than in another, and it cannot be that the lack of openness in some eu countries undermines the implementation of our regulation. i therefore call on the commission to come up with a directive which will force all eu member states to increase transparency and openness in governance. and i will certainly bring this point to the convention on the future of europe, of which i am a member. finally, mr president, i think it is important that we do not wait too long to evaluate this regulation. we have made great strides with this regulation, but there are certainly still some things to defend. the first evaluation will be at the end of this year and i hope to be involved again. but, mr president, the winners of this regulation are our own citizens. they will be able to obtain much more information than before, especially via the internet, and that is good for the reputation of parliament, good for the reputation of the european institutions and, above all, good for democracy in europe in general.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject of transparency. the european people have the idea of a europe that is secretive and undemocratic, where decisions are taken behind closed doors. the european convention has recently taken a very important step towards an open and democratic europe, partly through the open dialogue that this forum has with civil society organisations. the european union is also committed to the principle of subsidiarity, which is the basis for the european union's policy on the environment. we want a transparent form of european decision-making. access to documents is an essential part of this transparency. information exchange is the engine behind public debate in the media, public scrutiny and input from civil society organisations. that is why we in the european parliament have been fighting for some time to ensure public access to documents - not only documents of the european parliament, but also of the council and the commission. my colleague mr cashman, together with mrs maij-weggen, has also done a lot of good work in an earlier phase and we are now in the process of following up on that. it is important that we continue this struggle until documents which are currently considered to be non-public documents of the european institutions are also available to those who are interested or simply interested in them. mrs maij-weggen has rightly referred to a number of issues surrounding the solana decision which have not yet been properly translated into a complete replacement. she has rightly pointed out that we want to extend the list with a number of items, such as the attendance list, and that we do not want any restrictions and we support her in that. the idea of a directive - probably in a 'minimum way', because subsidiarity must be recognised in itself and each country must implement it in its own way, so that every citizen in his own country has a minimum of security in terms of access to documents - the rapporteur. the directive at issue is a directive known as the insolvency directive, but it is obviously a directive on the protection of workers, the social protection of workers in this case, when there is an insolvency of the employer and there are insufficient or no longer any financial resources to pay back arrears of wages. the insolvency directive provides important protection for employees when their employer is in financial distress. the existing directive is directive no 987 of 1980. it is clear that the insolvency directive prevents employees from fighting creditors for overdue payments. instead, they can avail themselves of the provisions of this insolvency directive. it is a revision of a directive, which in this case means that two very important improvements are being made, and we are satisfied with the content of it anyway. the amendments include the inclusion of parttime workers, fixedterm workers and temporary agency workers in the new directive. this is based on guidelines which have been in existence for these workers for some time and which have been developed in a social dialogue. it is a new category of workers and it is important that we pay attention to it, especially in the light of what is developing in the field of flexibilization of work and the need for it in the light of processes such as those in the framework of lisbon and so on. secondly, in situations where companies operate in more than one country, it is made clear where and how the directive is applied and in which country. the importance of this is obviously great, because we are slowly but surely seeing clearly what this means for workers, not only in spain, as was the case last year with the telefonica company, but also in german firms such as holzman and kirch. in 2001 the number of people unemployed as a result of insolvency cases increased sharply in europe alone. in total, 1.4 million people were affected by the bankruptcy of their employer. it is obvious that this is linked to many other things. the first reading, because we are talking about the second reading, has already adopted a number of amendments from the ep. in particular, the possibility of excluding certain categories of workers should be restricted and thresholds should no longer be applied in the form of a minimum duration of employment contract after which remuneration in accordance with the directive would be payable. it was also assumed at that time that the chapter on organization and financing, article 5 in the old directive, would be accepted. the council later agreed to accept the de facto situation of insolvency and agreed that an employee could claim unpaid wages from the fund in so far as this was provided for in national legislation. finally, following the second reading of the council, and in particular its common position, agreements were also reached on the application or non-application of ceilings in general. it is important in this connection that, because the labour market developments are not stagnant, we have asked questions about all kinds of new categories of workers which have been discussed for some time and for which we would actually like a definition of the concept of employer, employee, self-employed, self-employed without staff, etc. we therefore asked for the application of this directive to a number of selfemployed persons not mentioned earlier, such as selfemployed persons without staff, employees with a training contract, home workers, etc. we wanted to avoid the conciliation procedure if we were to get a commitment from both the commission and the council that this whole process of legalising this situation would be speeded up. finally, it was agreed that the commission would carry out a study of what is called 'new forms of work and employment relations' in both the member states and the candidate countries. i think this is an important development. we have also agreed that when this study is published, and this will be within a year and a half, the committee on social affairs and employment and the european commission will jointly hold a hearing to discuss the study and then to consider whether and to what extent there should be guidelines, framework directives and the like to solve this whole problem. i have again emphasized that we are talking about the need for new and comprehensive european labour legislation, especially in the context of the increasingly flexible labour market. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure follow-up procedure - the conciliation procedure - and has enabled us to reach good agreements. i hope the commissioner will give his opinion.

in writing. - (nl) unlike trains or buses, airplanes are totally dependent on the proper functioning of their engines. when an aircraft's engines fail for technical reasons or by accident, it crashes. the victims are not only the occupants of the aircraft but also the people living in the area where the debris of the aircraft crashes. we have seen such cases in the air disasters at lockerbie in scotland - it was an attack - and in the bijlmermeer area of amsterdam, caused by negligence and the refusal of publicity. safety is now subordinated to the way civil aviation is organised. different airlines compete with each other and try to control as large a share of the passenger market as possible by compressing costs and fares as much as possible. the fact that there is no charge for kerosene already gives these companies an advantage over overland transport. in most cases, they pass on the cost of security to the public authorities rather than incorporating it into the ticket price. mrs foster has become the airline spokesperson in this house and stresses the need to let the airline market develop without hindrance. i cannot support this litany of proposals which take for granted a model of organisation which is bound to lead to real disasters.

left behind. there were actually three main points at the conciliation stage. i'll run them over. parliament asked that the slightly lower noise levels be measured. this is important because experience in my country has taught us that if you measure only the high and the very high levels, you get a spread of the noise over much larger areas of the slightly less loud noise. parliament has achieved about half of what we wanted to achieve: just good luck with that. point number two: the target. the targeting has been significantly enhanced. the council of ministers is only talking about combating the negative effects. in plain english, it's called setting up noise barriers along motorways. but experience has taught me that you have to be much more structured. you have to deal with the sound yourself, with, for example, whispering tapes or whispering asphalt. it is a very important step forward. i am glad that the council has finally agreed that the objective should be to reduce noise and not just to combat and reduce its negative effects. finally, the most important and most controversial point: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the noise levels in the community are not exceeded. this is particularly the case with road traffic, which is the main source of noise, aircraft noise, train noise, but also noise from machinery outside the home and from machinery in factories whose noise penetrates outside the factory floor. parliament, and indeed the whole of parliament, asked for guidelines to deal with these sources as well and not just to measure them. this was not an absurd demand. as early as 1992, the fifth environmental action programme, written by laurens jan brinkhorst as the then chief environmental officer, stated that the commission would come up with a proposal for measurement in 1994 - the proposal did not come until 2000 - and that the commission would come up with the directives in 1995. the commission has never taken it out of the drawing-room for some reason, as it may be able to explain. the only thing parliament has said now, and fortunately the council has agreed, is that the commission will propose this subsidiary directive by 2006, 11 years later than it had announced. given the importance of the subject of noise, which concerns one third of europeans, european citizens, and in a very negative sense, i shall not make it difficult to deal with it and i hope that the commission, as we have also agreed, will come out with a sort of green paper in a year and a half on how to proceed with these subsidiary directives. i hope that in some areas, such as tyres, we will not have to wait four years before the commission comes forward with new proposals. i was going to leave it at that, considering the late hour.

in writing. - (nl) i should like to make the following statement in connection with the vote on the rothley report on the fixed price of books. most countries already have some form of fixed book price or are considering introducing it. in its resolution of february 2001, the european council stressed the particular cultural value of the book and its importance in promoting cultural diversity in europe. it therefore asked the european commission to take this into account when applying the competition rules and the rules on the free movement of goods and to intervene only in cases of intentional circumvention of existing national provisions on the fixing of book prices and where the movement of goods between member states was adversely affected. in its agreements with the german book industry of 22 march 2002, the european commission clearly listened to them. it therefore appears that the book enjoys a right to exist as a cultural object and falls within the scope of article 151 of the treaty. on this basis, i therefore believe that i must vote for mr rothley's report, in which he states that each member state is free to introduce or not to introduce a form of fixed price for books, but that agreements must be made at european level in the case of cross-border trade and especially in the case of intentional circumvention of national prices. the aim is to guarantee legal certainty for all market players through a stable economic and legal framework, but also, and just as importantly, to respect and promote cultural diversity, which includes the cultural property known as 'free'.

increasing the productivity and earning capacity of so-called disadvantaged groups. this is especially true of women. it is therefore a pity that this analysis has not been thought through to the end. we have tried in vain to understand that it is the unequal distribution of paid and unpaid work between men and women which is the basis of the overrepresentation of women among the poor. poverty among women is directly linked to their lack of economic independence. this should be promoted through paid work that provides a sustainable income for women themselves and for those who depend on them. if the commission and the member states are to follow us in this gender analysis, the degree of economic independence of women in europe will have to be re-examined and this factor will have to play an independent role in the analytical framework and policy objectives of anti-poverty policy. indeed, single older women and single mothers with young children are particularly vulnerable groups. but their vulnerability will not be reduced if the causes are not faced fairly. as long as women, and particularly women with children, are overburdened with unpaid work and are prevented from mr president, social exclusion is a difficult subject. the word itself gives rise to a great many differences. we know that the commission introduced the concept of social exclusion at the time because the word poverty was considered exaggerated by some member states. now we have a certain contradiction. one might imagine that there is a socially excluded millionaire. that's entirely possible, but that's not what we're talking about here. we are talking about money and everything that has to do with it. then, of course, there's the question: is poverty in europe not the same as poverty in the third world? no, it's not that. you have to compare people in europe with people in europe. you can't compare someone in bad circumstances to someone in the third world. that is too easy for governments. however, there is a problem, namely that under the system of subsidiarity most of these responsibilities are vested in the member states, and even in the municipalities. of course, we can give a lot of helpful advice on this. we can make deals and we can make comparisons. it's all possible. the problem can only be solved at the lowest possible geographical level. many people sometimes overlook this fact. it seems like we could solve the whole social exclusion problem here. that's not possible. we can exchange information, set good examples and agree on certain common issues to a certain extent, but those common issues must not be counterproductive. i think that in europe we have not improved the position of children by any means through a large number of ideologically motivated measures in the past. we should keep that in mind, too. we cannot do that, the member states must do that. we can only give a few wise lessons in that regard and we must leave it at that. i think the rapporteur has written a good report, but sometimes we have to learn a lesson from this.

in writing. - (nl) parliamentary immunity seems to be very important to many members because it is constantly discussed in this parliament. the national rules of their respective member states apply to meps and differ widely. in one country this means that members of parliament cannot, without their own cooperation or without a decision to waive their immunity, be prosecuted for offences committed during their term of office, and are therefore favoured over other citizens. it's convenient for criminals who want to protect themselves. in other countries, such as the netherlands, this only means that a member cannot be prosecuted on the basis of statements made, as a member, in the context of parliamentary debate or questions. for the moment, i am in favour of this limited concept of immunity, because it guarantees equality between members and their constituents, without them being able to be hindered in their work. i understand that in some states where there have often been attempts to seriously impede the work of parliamentarians considered to be enemies by constantly bringing legal proceedings against them, immunity is more necessary. but let us limit it as much as possible and not make it a european right.

in writing. - (nl) a parliament can function properly only if at least the following three conditions are met. first, parliament must at all times be a true reflection of the many views and interests of society, and at the same time be fed by society. secondly, there must be sufficient room for these differences to be expressed openly in the public debate, which occurs when members have the opportunity to react to each other and to ask for clarification by means of interruptions and a second round of discussions, before the decision is taken. thirdly, citizens must have the certainty that parliament can take the initiative itself and take final decisions by simple majority on legislation, the budget and the formation of coalitions. unfortunately, the european parliament does not meet any of these criteria and the proposed amendment to the regulation will not change that at all. the amendment concerns mainly the limitation of speaking time, the shortening of voting procedures by a stricter selection of amendments and the possibility for the president to give the floor on his own initiative to members of parliament who are sympathetic to him. these changes are to the advantage of both major groups and to the disadvantage of those who wish to put forward desirable or possible alternatives. the european parliament thus remains a senate, far from the people, whose main task is to justify its votes and to report on the facts.
in writing. - (nl) in view of the meticulously laid obstacles in the way of those who would like to form small groups, the european parliament has fewer groups than some national parliaments. this system has the advantage of having led to the formation of international groups of parliamentarians of more or less identical affiliation rather than to the creation of 150 groups each corresponding to national parties. however, there are disadvantages, such as the situation of some isolated members who do not find shoes on their feet or change groups regularly. in the netherlands i have always been used to a system where parliamentary groups are created by the results of elections. any list that wins seats, even if only one, is given group status. in the european parliament, on the other hand, groups are formed only after elections and the transfer of certain members to another group is not considered a theft. as the formation of a group requires the presence of many members from different member states, some political currents never reach the desired critical size. this has led to the creation of ideologically coherent groups in which there have long been practical disagreements because of divergent national public opinions, but also to the creation of artificial technical groups in which parties that do not know each other collaborate. similarly, the obligation for all members not knowing where to go to participate in a mixed group on the spanish model is in my view an aberration.
