- madam president, in 20 years the cod stock in the north sea has been reduced by three quarters. at the same time, the number of cod fishermen in my country has fallen considerably. in 1980, there were 310 cod anglers flying the dutch flag, but now most have switched to flatfish and there are still a handful of cod anglers left. however, this reduction in the number of fishermen is not enough. the commission is right to put forward proposals for multiannual recovery programmes for cod and hake. in the commission's proposals for reform of the european fisheries policy recently presented by commissioner fischler, we are missing precisely those reductions related to fish stocks. the relationship between cod and, to a lesser extent, hake is clear. i fully agree with mrs stihler when she says in the explanatory statement to the report that the priority must be to restore the stocks successfully. the package of measures must be effective, but it must also take account of the socioeconomic damage to the fisheries sector. it is not worth putting pressure on the sector unless the measures taken have a positive effect on stocks. it is therefore important to monitor the effectiveness of the measures. measures should be reversed as soon as it is clear that they are not having a positive effect. as a bad example of such a pointless measure, i would remind the commission of the cod emergency plan it put in place for the north sea in the winter of 2000. the emergency plan to close part of the north sea to fishing was counterproductive. in the open areas, fishing pressure increased dramatically, while in the closed areas, fish stocks were depleted very quickly after reopening. the closed areas did not correspond well to cod spawning areas, according to fisheries biologists. the concentration of the fleet in the open areas has led to overfishing of vulnerable land. fishermen and biologists, i think, rightly concluded that the commission was concerned less with efficiency and more with political feasibility. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. it is not possible that dutch fishermen who are allowed to catch 10% of the total allowed catch, the cod tac, are much more restricted in their fishing activities than british fishermen who are responsible for 40% of the tac. i would like to make a number of comments on the measures proposed by the commission. first of all: the aforementioned closures are an example of how not to do it. real-time closures, closures when an area is found to have a high concentration of juvenile fish, can be an efficient measure. technical measures may be of particular interest to fishermen who have cod as a by-catch. secondly: the reduction of the cod tacs risks a huge increase in fishing pressure on non-quota species. proactive policy should include quoting unquoted species as soon as possible. this is all the more important as spanish and portuguese vessels will also be sailing in the north sea in 2003. if the commission does not set tacs and quotas for these species, we can expect recovery plans for these species in 10 years' time. thirdly: an effort reduction is achieved as quickly as possible by applying the sea days regime. it is good to see that a system applied in the netherlands, which has always been criticized by the commission, is now finally being adopted by the same commission. i hope that the commission will apply this method more widely. a weekend ban, well known in the transport world, is recommended by dutch fishermen. fourthly: the commission should not simply leave the development of the sea days scheme and the financial compensation to the member states. this leads to unfair competition. the commission should set reduction rates for each member state. these figures may be based on quotas and observed overfishing in recent years. finally , we must be careful that fleets which have found a balance between effort and quota are not further repaired. i am referring to the fact that if a fleet is able to operate profitably and efficiently under good quota management, that should not be disturbed. it is good that the subsidy for new construction is being abolished. but even when fifg funds are used, care must be taken not to artificially maintain fishing capacity. it is important that the impact of the plans be evaluated in good time. it is also important that we take account of the socioeconomic damage to the sector. if the recovery plan fails, the damage to cod, hake and fishermen will be immense.

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, with thanks to the members of the committee on industry, in particular mr read and mr harbour, and to the secretariat of the committee on the environment, i am pleased to be drawing up this report as rapporteur. it concerns the accessibility of government websites, especially for disabled and elderly people. the contacts with the european commission have also been very fruitful. the commission's communication aims to draw attention to the web accessibility component of the lisbon strategy. in order to make websites accessible to disabled persons' equipment, it is necessary that they are designed in a technically correct way. to this end, the global consortium w3c has developed guidelines. member states have committed to applying these guidelines to government websites. the european commission is monitoring the progress of this process. since all citizens should have access to government information, the accessibility of public websites is of obvious importance. governments also have a special responsibility for the weakest members of society. the european parliament can therefore wholeheartedly support this process. it called for greater efforts to be made to implement the directive. otherwise, the objective mentioned by the commission, namely to achieve accessibility of public websites in 2003, will not be achieved in time. the user, for example a disabled employee in the public service, will, i hope, soon have unhindered access to government sites. it is also essential that this official can post information on a website himself. the software for putting information on the web must therefore also be accessible. however, a static end-point is not possible. internet technology is rapidly evolving. i therefore call for the guidelines to be developed in parallel with this technical dynamic. the governments will therefore have to follow developments closely. this brings us to the question of what these guidelines mean for public authorities today. first, accessibility for all must be part of the design process from the outset. secondly, accessibility for all requires that governments provide their information in a technology-neutral way. so not just on the internet. the question then is, of course, whether formal compliance with the guidelines will be effective and practical. the report therefore calls for the establishment of information points in the member states. users can submit their findings and complaints there. these signals from society will have to lead to improvements in the websites. there has been some debate as to whether a more binding nature of the guidelines would produce a better result. but it would not solve the core of the problem at the moment. the core of the problem is the unfamiliarity with the guidelines, not the possible unwillingness of web designers. i think that there is no reason at this stage to legislate at european level. the commission does, however, want to make private sites as accessible as soon as possible, alongside public ones. in the committee on industry there was a point of discussion as to which of the types of websites had the greatest urgency. since the field makes different sounds, it would be good to give priority to websites with the greatest relevance to the user groups. these can be both commercial websites and websites of social interest. moreover, those public interest websites also include websites of a commercial nature. think of shops, banks, and public transportation companies. the report also focuses on the candidate countries. the size of the objective still to be achieved means that accessibility is also worth a major effort in those countries. finally, mr president, the improvements will also have to be measurable in the field. the report therefore supports further research into measurable criteria for compliance with the guidelines. we were getting some hopeful signals from the field. the dutch bartiméus institute for the blind, which provided us with excellent advice, developed an initiative in this direction. it hopes to launch a website next week where people can sign up for a regular check of the website. this can be used to obtain a certificate of accessibility. the site will be launched in dutch. however, the arrival of an english version does not exclude the institute, so that non-dutch people can also test their sites. all in all, i look forward to a situation where disabled people have as much easy access to the medium of the internet as people without disabilities. i hope that this report will help to do that. the internet is a source of information and, not to mention, a means of communication which plays an increasingly important role in society as a whole. technological development should not exclude groups but rather assist their participation in society. good technology is, after all, in the service of man.

in writing. -(nl) in recent decades, all the attention has been paid first to the creation of national motorway networks and then to the construction and expansion of airports. it is only in recent years that most member states have invested in improving railways and sometimes also in inland waterways. however, some of these high-speed lines are being built at the expense of improving and maintaining short-distance rail transport. we do not know whether expensive railways, such as the betuwe line in the netherlands, will be used as long as companies are free to transport their goods more economically by road and the corresponding rail capacity is lacking in neighbouring countries. in relation to these controversial investments, it must be admitted that there is still no integrated european rail network that quickly crosses national borders, mountain ranges and straits. the rapporteur, mr turchi, is right to say that investment in railways and inland waterways is lagging behind and that there is too little progress in the construction of tunnels under the alps and the pyrenees. to stop the heavy truck traffic through these mountains and the long detours that passenger trains must make, these tunnels must be given priority. to this end, the extension of co-financing to 20% is acceptable, but cannot be required for all other types of projects. otherwise there will be nothing to distribute and stagnation will continue.
in the case of the united kingdom, the commission has already taken the initiative in the form of a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens. and the mixing with oil is frauds. even a biofuel, and an environmentally friendly one by comparison, can be used as a means of encouraging and justifying the growth of road traffic. opting for more public transport is preferable because this type of transport can more easily use hydropower, wind and solar energy. this energy remains the best choice of motive power for means of transport. plant products are naturally preferable to drilling and mining for minerals, which destroy and poison the landscape. the burning of these fossil fuels is a major contributor to global warming. more vegetable fuel means far more hectares of agricultural land to be exploited, and the intensive depletion of this land. the same area will be impossible to grow food for the growing world population. these fuels, which are considered environmentally friendly, are likely to increase agricultural land at the expense of already severely threatened tropical forests. nevertheless, lower taxes on biofuel, which causes fewer environmental problems, are provisionally justifiable as a means of influencing consumer and business behaviour. to do this, we do not actually need an eu regulation, because the member states must be able to do this independently. if the rapporteur proposes to strengthen this freedom, i agree with him.
in writing. -{nl) nuclear energy is very controversial but after a long pause following the harrisburg and chernobyl disasters, there is a renewed attempt to build new nuclear power stations. as long as nuclear energy exists, for peaceful or military purposes, the dangers will remain significant. the explosion or meltdown of the installations not only threatens life over a wide radius, but there are also dangerous radioactive residual products with incredibly long half-lives. it is precisely these waste products that are of interest to criminals and terrorists, who want to force capitulation by threatening to spread dangerous substances. in my opinion, the rapporteur is being overly optimistic when he thinks that he can avoid these types of problems altogether through better control. however, this control is imperative in the present circumstances. this is the most useful task for what remains of euratom, the european institution once set up to promote the large-scale use of nuclear energy. an independent nuclear safety and security office, which can directly monitor the safety of nuclear power stations and nuclear materials of all operators in the member states and in future member states, must certainly be set up. i also support the proposal to ban the production of nuclear weapons in the european union and to control it in order to prevent it.
- in the debate on genetically modified organisms we cannot confine ourselves to technical discussions, but must give emphasis to ethical aspects. we may use god's creation to satisfy our need for food. this does not mean, however, that we should be allowed to infringe the specific character of living nature. however, interested companies argue that biotechnology is necessary to solve the food shortage. the problem, however, is not that there is not enough food, but that it is not well distributed. moreover, lack of money is often the reason why people have no food. if we look at the famine in the southern african countries, it is clear that these problems cannot be solved by biotechnology. last year we adopted a directive which allowed the placing on the market of genetically modified food under certain conditions. the conditions are environmental and health protection, consumer choice and polluter pays. if industry cannot meet these conditions, we should still refrain from placing genetically modified food on the market. my concern is that despite the strict labelling requirements, genuine freedom of choice is not guaranteed. unintentional pollution will always occur. i also believe that non-gmo products should not be more expensive than gmo products.
- this is not the first discussion about food and gmos that i've been allowed to intervene in. i would remind you of the debate on the non-food regulation some five years ago. the position which my group and i took at that time was, firstly: gmos in food are allowed if the consumer so wishes, but then we must opt for a safe and transparent system where only gmos that are authorised and therefore safe can be used. secondly: there must be freedom of choice for the consumer. that means that the consumer must be given the best possible information, so that he can make his own choice. mr president, those two principles were the reason why we were so opposed to the 'may contain' label at the time of the non-food regulation. the may contain label does not inform, it does not make anyone wiser. we have, or rather i have introduced an amendment on behalf of our group to the non-food regulation that if genetically modified dna is found in food, it must be labelled. i remember the food industry protests of that time and i also remember very well the support of many organisations, including the dutch consumer organisation at the time. the consumer has no choice in the proposal we are discussing today, mr president, nor in the current practice, despite claims to the contrary. - why? - why? very simple because in the so-called trash hold, a minimum of one percent of the modified dna in the food can be found, without labelling. for the sake of clarity, the european commission now confirms this non-labelling below one percent. so that means that there are foods on the market that are not labeled and yet have almost one percent altered dna. the european commission's proposal before us today makes consumer choice even more opaque. i'll explain it to you. the principle of analytical detectability in the final product has been abandoned. we have always wanted this principle, with the 1% threshold, below which there is no labelling. the new requirement is that all additives to the final product on paper derived from or processed with gmos must now be labelled. in practice, this may mean that if a fruit juice bottle has been treated with sugar, vitamin c or a filler, and it is established on paper that it is made from gmo maize after many stages of processing, the fruit juice bottle will have to be labelled as genetically modified. mr. president, this is bizarre. a paper thousandth of altered dna has to be labeled, whereas the bottle without that vitamin c doesn't have to be labeled, whereas it can still contain one percent altered dna. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the labelling of products is not subject to any restrictions. i call the cheese on the pizza, the milk in the chocolate bar. mr president, i think that the introduction of paper tigers is a deception of the consumer. that is the only reason why i am against this proposal. what i will continue to work hard for with my colleagues is honest, objective and demonstrable information for consumers, which really gives them the opportunity to choose.

in writing. - (nl) this subject seems to be primarily a technical matter which does not involve any important political choice. this is not the case, because the consequences can be significant, both for consumer protection and for the well-being and health of workers. the european machinery directive pursues two essentially opposite objectives. on the basis of article 95 of the treaty, which relates to the internal market, this directive must be able to promote the free movement of goods. fortunately, paragraph 3 of that article also refers to a high level of protection of public health, safety and consumer protection, and the question is whether this is the case. although research on this subject is still insufficient, it seems that the current directive has not led to a significant reduction in the number of accidents at work. i do not expect any major results from the revision of the directive, and certainly not if its application remains confused. the first limitation is that the highest value is given to voluntary certification, so-called european conformity, accompanied by a ce marking, which offers less guarantees than the old national certification authorities, such as kema, responsible for the certification of electrical appliances in the netherlands. the second reason is that vehicles, switches, generators, escalators and small lifts are excluded from the directive.

in writing. - (nl) no one really knows what the subject of parttime use of real estate is. this proposal concerns measures to prevent fraud and embezzlement. some citizens think that they can buy a holiday home for a low price for the exact period during which they intend to go on holiday, while other tourists own the same home for other periods. since these are often places of residence in a region where the language, customs, and laws differ from those of the owners' home country, the risk of misunderstanding is high. much worse still: it is easy to deceive buyers. since they cannot manage this accommodation themselves because of their long absence, someone must do it for them. it is the seller who remains the de facto owner. buyers are disappointed because they have to pay large sums of money and can only claim a few rights. eventually, they end up with a property that doesn't live up to their expectations and they can't sell it to anyone. the same measures are needed in the various european countries against this cross-border fraud. the opponents of centralistic and interventionist community legislation, including myself, also find this a useful form of consumer protection.
in writing. - (nl) one of the characteristics of capitalism is that enterprises are also commercial commodities. large companies that make large profits can buy other companies. sometimes these acquisitions are made to close the company in question and recover its market share. the profits can also be used to exclude competitors from the market by temporarily lowering prices, with the aim of driving them into bankruptcy. the concentration of wealth and power is an integral part of the logic of capitalism. so we can expect that an increasingly small number of companies will survive as they become larger and more international. in itself, it is not always a problem for a firm to achieve a monopoly position. monopolies for supplying a single region, with sales prices, environmental policy and social policy under democratic control by popular representation and the relevant citizens' representative organisations, can work very well. however, such monopolies are now destined for demolition within the eu - following the us example - on the grounds that they impede free competition, even though large concentrations of power free from any form of democratic control can continue to flourish. twelve years of application of regulation 4064/89 have not been able to put an end to it, nor will the forthcoming revision or the cooperation with the national competition authorities. i do not, however, reject this green paper, because inaction would be much worse.
in writing. - (nl) the organization of fishing at sea differs greatly from one country to another. while one country uses small traditional vessels, the other uses large modern vessels, which, to compensate for their size, have to stay in port for part of the campaign. fishermen in some countries catch fish for human consumption, while fishermen in other countries produce fish meal. and everywhere, fishermen from one country blame overfishing on those from another, so that stocks are collapsing in a growing number of regions. and now we are hearing that the netherlands produces illegible annual reports, belgium uses incomprehensible codes, spain does not produce enough and france does not produce any reports at all. the control regulation is applied differently in the different member states, which leads to unequal treatment of fishermen. it is becoming increasingly clear that, while we boast of reducing fishing effort substantially, this is hardly the case. and in the meantime there is a revolt in the making against the european commission's proposals to give substance to and strengthen the policy of protecting fisheries resources. so, it probably won't work this time either. so the policy is to say "after me, the flood". do the laxists think that such a flood will bring more fish?
in writing. - (nl) it is striking to see how different the controls of traffic offences are in europe. while one country increases speed limits, the other controls only serious offences. the application is not community, but the fisheries policy is. unfortunately, the checks on fishermen are as varied as those on road safety. what is worse, national inspection services seem to punish fishermen from neighbouring member states more severely than those from their own country for the same offence. the differences between member states as regards the nature and frequency of controls and penalties undermine the common fisheries policy. the dutch fishermen are rightly calling for a european inspection and control structure. the harmonization of control and sanction policy is essential: it is the credibility of fisheries policy that is at stake. the dutch producer organisations shall carry out mutual checks on the exceedance of quotas. this example should be followed in the other member states. it is still absurd that we do not know whether all european fishermen are respecting the quotas or not.

the commission has already made a number of proposals. the european packaging directive has brought a lot into play. we sort and collect our waste. recycling plants are now established all over europe. people all over europe are working to recycle the waste that we all produce. hard and intensive work. we're all doing this for the environment, and we have to keep doing it, because the waste mountain is still growing. but we must not close our eyes to some of the difficulties of the packaging directive. firstly, there are major differences between member states in the implementation of the packaging directive. this is sometimes due to laxity, but often also to real problems, such as lack of sales opportunities. secondly, the environmental return is not always clear. we think recycling is good for the environment, but there's a limit to it. for example, if the distance is too long, the environmental benefit becomes a disadvantage. thirdly, we still see a lot of unnecessary packaging. packaging has an essential function, of course, to protect the product, but a double layer of plastic for a small piece of bread is a bit excessive. these issues were raised in parliament's resolution last year. it is against this background that we have dealt with the commission proposal. we support the commission's amendment, but we think it is too restrictive. the prevention aspect in particular has hardly been worked out. colleagues, we have had a lot of discussion on this. i thank all my colleagues and especially the shadow rapporteurs for their contributions. the environment committee can present a result that provides good starting points for further steps towards sustainable development. i will make a few points. firstly, the environmental result of the directive, which unfortunately is not always clear. the environmental impact must be clear to continue to motivate citizens to separate their waste. the committee on the environment therefore calls for a clear evaluation of the environmental performance of the packaging directive. the environmental outcome must not only be clear to citizens, but also be at the forefront of the choices made by businesses and governments. we must lay the foundations here, and that brings me to my second point: the prevention of accidents. manufacturers choose the packaging for a product based on essential functions and within these are choices. soft drinks can be packaged in cardboard, metal, glass, plastic, or a combination of these. the environmental management committee asks producers to choose the most environmentally friendly alternative. an indicator should be established for this purpose. this packaging environment indicator shall consist of at least two parameters: the amount of waste and greenhouse gas emissions. greenhouse gas emissions are a global problem and therefore should be given equal weight in each country. however, the waste problem and recycling capacity vary from country to country and therefore the values allocated should also vary from country to country. the environmental indicator for packaging has been the subject of considerable debate. one effect is clear. different materials such as paper, metal, glass and plastic must compete with each other on the basis of environmental quality. so there is an incentive for constant innovation in the environmental field, an incentive to invest in recycling capacity. this leads to an optimal recycling capacity in each country. it's important that we take the first step now. the industry wants clear political statements that at least indicate a direction. my third point concerns recycling. until the prevention policy is fully operational, we must work on the recycling targets. the problem with the recycling target is that it is never optimal for all countries. what is ambitious for the united kingdom and spain is not ambitious for germany or austria. i think the 65% proposed by the committee on the environment is a good compromise for the first reading. there's been a lot of debate about whether or not material-specific goals are appropriate. and i'm also suggesting a middle ground here: the commission has not yet adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment against the risks arising from the use of certain substances or mixtures of substances. at least 25% for plastics and wood and 60% for the rest. member states will then have sufficient choice to achieve the best possible rates. as for the maximum targets, this was a great idea in the early days of recycling but now it's absolutely not necessary. there are no longer any market distortions caused by excessive national targets. the next point concerns recycling. the debate on reuse is mainly concerned with beverage packaging and has been re-ignited in a number of countries. mostly in germany, denmark and the netherlands. the reuse of waste is also the subject of most of the internal market problems. recycling is often a benefit for local producers of beer or mineral water. it is, in fact, improper use of recycling and we must prevent it. that is why we must also put the environmental result first. member states should encourage reuse where it is more environmentally friendly. the last point concerns the heavy metals. it is clear to everyone that these must be abolished. the committee on the environment has voted for the zero line. it has been pointed out that this hinders the use of recycled materials and that is not our intention, of course. we therefore want to make it clear that the use of heavy metals must be zero. finally, ladies and gentlemen, a word on sustainable development. in johannesburg, the world is talking about sustainable development. today we have the opportunity to put this beautiful concept into practice. the concept of sustainable development must be given a new lease of life. we should clean up our own garbage instead of exporting it to developing countries. that is why we must work on producer responsibility. we have done this before in the directive on electronic waste and in the directive on scrapped cars. the responsibility for producers is not just financial. the producers must innovate on the environmental quality of their packaging. innovation is also the best guarantee for maintaining employment in the packaging sector. it is the best guarantee that the generations after us will not be burdened with our waste, with a lack of natural resources and with climate change. we hope that the revision of the packaging directive will contribute to this. i thank you for your attention and look forward to the debate.

commission. - (es) mr president, first of all, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr blokland, once again for his excellent report which he is presenting to us today. we are trying to see whether it is possible to provide economic incentives to companies to take account of the noise nuisance caused by certain aircraft, following the principle of rewarding the best and punishing the worst. although aircraft noise is already integrated into some community airport fee systems, the criteria used for differentiating and quantifying noise nuisance vary widely between member states. it is therefore difficult to compare one system with another. this proposal addresses this issue by providing a common framework for the classification of aircraft noise which enhances convergence and transparency, and allows for prediction of the situation in each individual case. the proposal is limited to the minimum necessary to achieve its objective and leaves sufficient scope for member states to adjust to specific parameters of certain airports, such as the level of the unit noise charge, the characteristics of the fleet serving a given airport, or the variation between the highest and lowest rate. the responsibility for the decision to impose noise charges is left to the member states. there is no obligation to levy charges at all airports, as there is no need to levy charges at those which do not have noise problems. i would like to thank parliament for its support for this dossier and, at the end of the debate, i will now comment in more detail on some of the amendments, stating that, once again, we will accept most of those tabled.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the noise levels at airports are not exceeded. although we have been fighting aircraft noise for years, it is still possible for large noise-makers to land at european airports. we think, for example, of the aircraft with a hush-kit, which are only just meeting the standard for chapter 3 aircraft, the so-called marginally compliant aircraft. other aircraft can also cause a lot of inconvenience, especially at large airports where many planes land and take off. to counteract the negative effects of these noisy aircraft, measures should be taken around airports, such as moving runways, installing sound barriers, moving residential areas, insulating houses and the like. it will be clear that these measures will require a great deal of money and effort. these costs should be borne by means of noise charges. aircraft noise is already an element in the charging system of a number of airports in europe. the present report aims at harmonizing noise charges at airports. the aim is, of course, to promote the use of quieter aircraft. the present common european framework provides for the calculation of noise charges in an easily understandable manner. this shall promote transparency, fairness and predictability and shall prevent arbitrariness. i would like to stress that noise charges based on measurements are not possible. at airports, we deal with other sources of noise and with planes that arrive or depart simultaneously. this directive therefore also uses a calculation method, since this is the only possible method. in order to avoid distortions of competition, the environmental committee has decided to apply the noise levy to all airports. however, there is more flexibility built into it. the difference between the highest and the lowest charge in a daily allowance may be multiplied by a factor of 40 instead of 20. in addition, it is established that the biggest noise makers pay more for their greater nuisance. the commission proposal makes it possible for the noisiest aircraft not to have to pay a higher noise charge than the quieter category. i believe that there is now sufficient flexibility built in. i therefore do not think it necessary to create an exception for airports which have a strict policy on noise charges. within the framework indicated by the committee on the environment, a very strict policy is possible. i do not think there are any airports which have such a strict policy that they are outside the scope. if we are going to treat some airports differently, it will be arbitrary. as indicated earlier, the proceeds from noise charges will be used to make investments that reduce noise pollution. however, the committee on the environment considers that other costs, such as environmental costs due to noise pollution, should also be paid. in addition, not all the effects of noise pollution can be expressed in exact terms. examples of this are disturbed sleep or psychological effects due to noise nuisance, which may be compensated financially. finally, it must be realised that the purpose of the noise charge is mainly to promote quieter aircraft. i would like to make one final comment on the amendments tabled by the green group. the use of noise standards for the calculation of the noise tax does not fit at all into the system of this directive. moreover, it is questionable whether these standards will ever be achieved. for these reasons, i do not support these amendments. mr president, i hope that this report will make noise charges fairer and more transparent. but i think it is much more important that the noise pollution for our citizens will be reduced.

in writing. - (nl) i did not support the deva report for several reasons. first, the demand to stop all subsidies in the eu is unilateral. i am in favour of the removal of barriers to third country products. but there are also good reasons for regional production or environmental subsidies. the effect on developing countries, while essential, is not the only consideration. in this context, it would be sensible for the wto to take into account in trade rules the extent to which the consumption of a specific product harms creation, starting with the production process and including transport to the country of consumption. a second critical point is the interpretation of the ethical investment theme. the report is a step in the wrong direction. it interferes with the internal organisation of enterprises when it prescribes the establishment of an internal committee within the enterprise and the sections of the enterprise to which this committee is to report. it would be more desirable to identify strategies to introduce ethical investment on a larger scale. in particular, the measurable character and the reporting system should be improved. finally, the call for a review of community public health policy is misplaced since public health is not a community competence.

in writing. - (nl) packaging is what a consumer keeps after buying a new product. packaging has become increasingly important over time, not only to protect the contents of the boxes but above all to attract the attention of potential buyers. packaging materials have become increasingly colourful and contain, in addition to the simple cardboard boxes of the past, materials which are harmful to the environment, such as heavy metals. it is high time that the commission proposed to amend the directive on packaging and packaging waste adopted eight years ago, but the proposed improvement is not enough. the emphasis on energy production by incineration is wrong, because it only allows the producers and processors of polluting packaging to continue in the old way. emphasis should be placed on waste prevention and the reuse of materials. the committee on the environment rightly wants at least 65% of the weight to be recycled, a total ban on the use of lead, cadmium, mercury or hexavalent chromium from 2007 and stricter requirements for new packaging materials from 2004. it is also a good proposal to aim to produce 10% less packaging waste in 2006 than in 1998 and to reassess national and european rules as to the obstacles they create to reuse.
in writing. - (nl) there is an increase in scale in all areas dealt with by the eu, often with the consequence of a decrease in the democratic involvement of citizens and a lack of good tailor-made solutions. that is why my opinion on this increase in scale is generally negative. i'll make an exception for the air force. these are most often cross-border and long-distance links. the maintenance of national control systems and the fragmentation of airspace into small areas would not contribute to safety. it would therefore be natural to entrust the whole of this task to the existing eurocontrol agency, which has long controlled the airspace of the benelux countries and western germany. this should also apply to military air traffic, which still has the possibility, especially in france, of reserving an unacceptably large part of the airspace. unfortunately, this chance for a clear and safe management of airspace has now been lost. if airspace is given away for a fixed period, the old fragmentation is perpetuated in another way. the geographical breakdown is being replaced by economic breakdown. i shall be looking into this in connection with mrs sanders-ten holte's report.
in writing. - (nl) on the fava report, i said that although the increase in the scale is probably inevitable, unfortunately the wrong choices are now being proposed again. the compulsory award of public tasks to private companies in mutual competition for a limited period of time, which has already been proposed previously for public transport and ports, is now also being put forward as a solution for the organisation of aviation safety. this means that each airspace block can "land" in another company, although in practice and in the long run a quasi-monopoly will emerge, controlling most of the airspace. so the neoliberal ideology is more important than security. in this model, the main concern is not safety but cost reduction. the hope is to achieve this cost reduction by working with fewer staff and in deteriorating working conditions. as they are divided among different companies with divergent interests and are constantly concerned about their chances of winning or losing the next tender, these people feel that their work is no longer as indispensable as it once was. this will inevitably result in a decline in the quality of their work. moreover, the military occupation of the airspace is still not lifted. i do not support this approach.

in writing. - (nl) the committee on agriculture and rural development is rightly concerned about the growing need to import soybean meal, much of it genetically modified, from the united states, brazil and argentina. these imports of animal feed now amount to almost twice the european domestic production. the old solution of feeding cows animal meal and slaughterhouse waste as a protein supplement has not worked since the mad cow crisis, or bse, but this is the only change that seems to be generally accepted today. we still dare not question the way in which we produce our food in general. so is it really reasonable to feed a plant-based food to pigs and then eat those pigs when the meat from those animals has a lower nutritional value than the original product? is it really reasonable to lift the ban on the addition of fishmeal to animal feed in order to add protein? the seas are overfished and fishermen in the south now react to all proposals for catch limits, always with the counter-argument that the north is guilty because it produces fish meal. a better part of the proposal is to include more leguminous and oilseed crops in the crop rotation.

- for a layman in the field of european regulation, it is a great and impenetrable mystery. many different schemes, varying requirements and conditions, numerous provisions and long texts form a forest of rules. without expert help, citizens and businesses are no longer able to find their way around. european legislation is not therefore distinguished by its clarity and uniformity. the fact that this leads to problems in support issues is shown by court cases and legal questions from local authorities, businesses and concerned citizens. the proposal to simplify and clarify the rules for granting aid for employment promotion therefore merits parliament's approval. simplifying and clarifying does not mean adding a lot of new, difficult to implement objectives and ideas. i would therefore like to make a brief comment on the first amendment. the additions in amendment no 1 belong to employment policy. they have no place in a resolution on aid under the ec treaty. in my view, the commission's regulation primarily regulates the financial side of aid. aid is granted only when it is necessary and the circumstances warrant it. the amendments mentioned in the first amendment are therefore, in my view, too broad for specific application in the context of aid. with the exception of amendment no 1, i therefore support this resolution. i agree with mr bouwman that the procedure followed in this report is rather strange.

in writing. - (nl) today, people are seen mainly as consumers. they must try to earn as much money as possible by long, hard work or speculation. anyone who fails to get rich quickly, often at the expense of his fellow man or the environment, is viewed as a failure. on the other hand, winners are constantly encouraged to spend all their winnings as quickly as possible with real estate agents, expensive vacation planners, and casinos. and regulations so that they are not dependent on the normal infrastructure of education, health care and public transport, because these are reduced, by savings, to a level acceptable only to the losers. no wonder the happy consumer is bombarded by advertising, including from abroad. this proposal is based on the principle that sales promotions such as discounts, gifts and competitions are beneficial to well-being. in 2000, they accounted for one million jobs in nine member states and more than €40 billion in expenditure. while even the liberal rapporteur, mr beysen, must admit that these sales promotions have negative consequences for book publishing and for the fair distribution of medicines, and that they encourage the addiction of young people to alcohol or to gambling machines, his proposal is not about consumer protection but about postponing the rules and reducing the number of constraints on business administrations. that is why i am voting against.
in writing. - (nl) within the eu, "state aid" has become a dirty word. partly right. state aid can mean that tax money collected by all of us for community tasks is paid to the cronies of certain politicians in power to ensure them an unjustifiable privilege. more often, on the contrary, state aid was a means of protecting vulnerable regions, disadvantaged occupational categories and essential public infrastructure. or to protect society from the consequences of major economic crises. for example, after the 1929 crash, there was an attempt to revive the economy by means of large investments, following the keynesian model. even these forms of aid are now treated as a form of distortion of competition because they are contrary to the liberal principle of competition and to the reduction of public expenditure. in these circumstances, any regulation which allows small pieces of state aid seems an improvement over outright liberalisation which makes the problems entirely impossible to solve. unfortunately, this proposal, which focuses on vulnerable groups of workers in small and mediumsized enterprises, is immediately weakened by a plea for further flexibility in the labour market. less protection of workers is therefore advocated as the best route to more employment, and aid only as an extreme means in case of emergency. that is why i think we should vote against it.

president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, 1996 was the european year of lifelong learning. now it is 2002, and in the netherlands over a million people are still functionally illiterate. i think that the situation in other member states will not be much better. it is not for nothing that the european union - and i congratulate the commissioner - is paying so much attention to this. perhaps it would be a good idea to organize a world summit on functional illiteracy in brussels after the johannesburg summit. after the memorandum and the definition of the strategy and priorities, we are now ready to create a european area for lifelong learning. that has my warm support. my group has always supported the previous reports by the rapporteur and i should like to thank her for her thorough report. two minor points, however. continuing education is a broad concept, ranging from the acquisition of appropriate social skills to highly technical training courses, from nursery schooling to university education. it is open to all, to all governments, to all public institutions. i would like to stress, however, that we must not lose sight of the quality of education. perhaps a quality assessment programme should be set up for this, as in mainstream education. i therefore support the call for the exchange of information, experience and best practice at european level and for the establishment and maintenance of a european database. the support of the european commission is of course essential. in addition, this will eventually lead to mutual recognition of credits, certificates and diplomas, which is very important for mobility. i would also like to stress the importance of the individual's own responsibility for his or her own education. he or she must decide whether to work on it and thus increase their chances on the labour market.
mr president, i hope to be 60 next year. an age i used to think you could retire to. but the opposite is true. i just have to keep learning new things to keep doing my job. and not just to do my job. also, to communicate with my children and grandchildren via e-mail, i need to keep up with the latest developments. i still learn new things every day with my computer. lifelong learning is therefore not a policy ideal but a fact. i agree with the need for lifelong learning. i believe that the active attitude of the public authorities is necessary to enable citizens to be constantly updated. the current policies in many member states fall short of this. the measures are aimed at employers, municipalities and benefit agencies, but not at stimulating the individual citizen. the best approach is one where the government pays for the education a person receives before entering the labour market. after that, employees should be responsible for their own development. the government and employers must then provide the right conditions and financial support. we can then work together within europe to shape these framework conditions to ensure the continuing participation of citizens in the labour market. even in their second childhood.
president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank mrs gutiérrez very much for the effort she has put into writing this owninitiative report. i fully agree with her that knowledge is the key to competitiveness and economic and social development in europe, but i certainly do not share all her conclusions. universities play a very important role in making europe the most dynamic and competitive knowledge-based economy. it is therefore very important that they keep in touch with each other and exchange information and experience. it is a question of providing high quality education, with the aim of creating centres of excellence in the university world. i fully agree with mrs gutiérrez that there is still a lot of room for improvement in the mobility of students, teachers and researchers. many administrative obstacles can be removed. but i do not see the point in the commission and the member states promoting the creation of a seat for european universities. i am not sure what role a representation of the member states and the european parliament should play in this. another point which i do not see the point of is the setting up of a separate european cultural university. literature, philosophy and communication are already taught at the existing universities, while special academies also exist for the arts. the report stresses the need for intercultural dialogue with the other regions of the world. yes, of course, but it suggests that the existing universities are completely closed in on themselves and have no contact with the rest of the world, and that's just an outdated idea. i am therefore afraid, mrs gutiérrez, that my group, although we agree with certain aspects of the report, will abstain from voting, as it cannot agree with the two points mentioned above.
in writing. - (nl) i do not like the promotion of citizenship of the union, the main objective of this proposal. in the former soviet union, attempts were made to merge citizens of the different states, with different languages and cultures, into soviet citizens. it never worked. in yugoslavia, an attempt was made to create, together with the serbs, croats, slovenes and macedonians, new generations of genuine yugoslavs who were to organise the future of the country. they're now second-class citizens. the creation of european citizens constantly travelling between member states in search of the most privileged jobs will lead to conflicts with their environment and to misfortune for themselves. a second objective of this proposal is to increase participation in european elections. people will not vote to satisfy a ritual obligation that they themselves do not see the utility of. they only want to vote when the body they are to elect exercises decision-making power and when there is a real choice between opposing alternatives. asking people to come and vote just because they are in favour of a united europe does not work. if we continue on this path, the next round of elections will bring even fewer voters. i can of course support strengthening the rights of citizens, including immigrants, and better information on the ombudsman.
in writing. - (nl) the absence of a right to participate has two causes. the first is an authoritarian conception of the state where citizens are seen only as conscripts and obedient taxpayers, who must leave the actual decision-making to an elite elected for that purpose, who know far better than the ordinary people how to do it. the other reason is economic interest. the protection of the environment from pollution, nuisance and hazards that most people want often implies an obstacle to the pursuit of profits for companies. this also leads to an authoritarian approach, where economic interests decide instead of the citizens as a whole. in recent decades, these barriers seem to have been broken. there are forms of citizen participation everywhere and the european union also recommends them. unfortunately, the results of such participation are still too often reversed. i support mrs korhola in her attempt to put an end to the exceptions which are still made at present for military interests and civil disasters. the military still often have the idea that they are above civil society and can impose their own considerations. disaster prevention measures are often very radical, such as flooding of polders in the event of rising river levels in the netherlands. we cannot make a decision on this without participation.
in writing. - (nl) in recent years the river regions of the rhine, the oder, the wilsa and the elbe have been successively affected by flooding. this is no coincidence. these rivers carry rainwater and meltwater from the alps and the carpathians to the north sea and the baltic sea. rainfall is increasing due to global warming, deforested soil is no longer able to hold water and riverbeds have become too narrow. along these channeled rivers, the dikes are located too close to the main watercourse and houses have been built on the banks where the water used to flow freely during floods. so there is no chance, these are predictable incidents. the need to implement the kyoto agreements at the global level has been rightly mentioned, but there is a fear that the us will continue to put the wheels in motion under pressure from oil companies and the automobile industry until it itself becomes the victim of increasing destruction and flooding. the focus is once again on the release of funds to help flood victims. it is necessary but not sufficient. in the next few years, the same disasters may happen again and unfortunately this is more than likely. our management of watercourses will therefore have to change drastically and even now, this point is still too likely to be neglected.

- mr president, the asylum system is under pressure and to solve this problem we must give priority to a common immigration policy. the report by mr evans falls flat on its face in paragraph 1. the pressure on the asylum system is indeed great. many asylum seekers are turning up at the gates of europe. experience shows that most of them do not fall within the definition ofrefugee in the geneva convention. the concept of 'refugee' has been interpreted in different ways and member states have developed secondary forms of protection. the difficulty of getting closer is shown by the negotiations in the council on the concept of refugee. it is therefore appropriate to compare and contrast the laws and policies of the member states on the basis of the guidelines proposed by the european commission, in order to move forward in mutual cooperation. however, the solution proposed in paragraph 1 of the evans report seems to me to be incorrect for a number of reasons. it's a weird circular argument, of course. the member states of the european union, for their own reasons, do not have an active immigration policy. the asylum system is overburdened by the fact that many people who are effectively immigrants are trying to enter the union through the asylum system. they are labeled with the confusing label "economic refugees". should we solve this problem by adopting an active immigration policy? that looks like carrying water to the sea to me. first of all, it must be stated that these people have no right to asylum. the idea of an immigration policy can then be discussed in substance. is that what we want for the european union? i think that there are very different views in the member states. this is also reflected in the reactions to the commission's communication on an open method of coordination for community immigration policy. the dutch government, for example, does not explicitly regard labour migration as an end in itself. studies by the dutch government have shown that this form of migration is not the solution to the ageing population and labour market bottlenecks in the netherlands. i can imagine that this may be different for other regions in the union, but there is certainly no simple general policy to be drawn up here. besides, it doesn't solve anything. in fact, it is not the asylum system that becomes the way to enter the european union, but the immigration system. even if the pressure from the asylum system were to ease, it would spill over into the immigration system at the same rate, creating the same abuses. there is no easy solution to the problem. the best paragraph in the report is the one that calls for an integrated approach to asylum and migration, trade, development, the environment and agriculture. because as long as the gap between rich and poor is this wide, people will continue to try to take the first step toward a better future for themselves and their children. this is a solution that will only bear fruit in the very long term, but there is no better one. in the meantime, we in the european union will have to continue to reflect on the practical implementation of our asylum and immigration policies. the notions of mercy and justice should be our guiding principles. mercy in the reception of refugees who have been driven from their own country. that means reception under humane conditions, as the report also stresses. at the same time, there must be justice. that's not always easy. because it means justice in the form of access to the justice system, but also in the form of rejection and expulsion. the exclusion clauses, which are very topical in the light of the events of 11 september 2001, also fall under the term 'justice'. of course, these should be used with restraint and caution. but admitting people who have nowhere else to turn is actually dangerously naive. if we want to ensure the safety of our citizens, we will apply those provisions. because it's been hanging on to that for the last few years. the netherlands seemed to make it almost a sport to provide shelter for people who were not received in other states. now they'll find out what they brought into the house. so , what do you say ? i agree with a restrictive and cautious application, but please, with the necessary sense of reality. sadly, the world is not a paradise filled with well-meaning people.

in writing. - (nl) authoritarian governments have always been characterised by the idea that the best way for them to survive criticism is to restrict the freedom of their citizens to exchange information, express opinions, organise and move about. the fear of terrorist attacks, which was born a year ago, brings to the fore old initiatives aimed at strengthening the army, the police and the secret services while limiting rights and freedoms. for some time now, this fear has made these controversial plans more acceptable to a wider public than at other times. the population is also discovering the disadvantages of such a development. in the netherlands, an action last week by computer users against the council's requirement to back up e-mail received over 2 500 signatures in two days. in addition to this breach of postal secrecy, which has been going on for over a century, we are witnessing attempts to cut the grass under the feet of radical opposition movements and force them to resort to violence, after which it becomes possible to declare them illegal. political organizations in exile in europe are being deprived of their right of residence and cut off from financial transactions. fortunately, this parliament is beginning to realise that the fear of terrorism cannot justify the suppression of the democratic and tolerant character of our societies. i oppose the proposal but support the proposals to improve the protection of personal data, to inform the ep and to make reports public.
in writing. - (nl) during the cold war, refugees from the east were more than welcome in western europe. flight was considered an act of love of freedom, an act with which everyone had to be in solidarity. at present, refugees are more likely to come from more distant destinations, they do not look like western europeans and the population shows less understanding of the situation they are fleeing. as the standard of living in the country they leave is always lower than ours, they are immediately suspected of fleeing for economic reasons. in the last 12 months, another fear has come to exacerbate this situation, that of being infiltrated by refugees who are nothing but terrorists. eu member states tend to limit the maximum number of refugees that can be allowed to enter their territory and to set their capacity below that of their neighbours. they are thus creating a fortress europe where even people in critical situations cannot enter, in violation of international treaties. as a result, more families are torn apart than ever before, and people are sent back to a country where they are not safe and are at risk of losing their lives. i disagree with the guideline but support the proposals of the committee on civil liberties and human rights, justice and home affairs that no one should be handed over to the authorities of countries where the death penalty is threatened, that refugee status should be refused only to war criminals and that the growing number of women among asylum seekers should be taken into account.

- mr president, the creation of the solidarity fund is in principle supported by us. however, the amended proposal as it is now presented will lead in the long run to an unsustainable financial situation within the current budgetary arrangements. the concept of a 'major disaster' is hardly defined and if damage does not exceed the threshold, there are generous exceptions. it is a lack of responsibility, in my view, to set up this fund in such a way. the citizens concerned may then be able to feel a warm feeling of eu solidarity, and in the end they themselves turn to the emergency aid they have received. to avoid such a hopeless situation, the fund must be streamlined. this means limiting the fund to natural disasters and adapting the thresholds and exceptional situations to the complementary nature of the fund. this is to avoid rewarding negligence, to encourage preventive measures, to make the best use of existing international compensation schemes and to guarantee the effectiveness of the fund. mr president, i was the only one in the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism who held this view. i therefore foresee major problems when the financial balance is drawn up after a number of years. i doubt whether there will be any solidarity between the states. for those who doubt that with me, i warmly recommend our amendments. otherwise, i'll place my hopes in the wisdom of the council. i would like to add, mr president, that i am pleasantly surprised by the acoustics in this chamber. it's probably to do with the extra equipment that's here. i can assure you it works very well.
commission. – mr president, i am pleased to be able to address the european parliament on the emissions trading proposal. i am proud of this proposal because i see it as a cornerstone of the european union's cost-effective implementation of the kyoto protocol. first, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr moreira da silva, for his unstinting efforts in bringing this proposal to its first reading. i know there were approximately 500 amendments in committee, but we now have a much more manageable 100 amendments for the commission's position on the amendments, see annex.. in february 2002, this house gave a resounding endorsement of the kyoto protocol. we in the european union were the first of the developed countries to ratify the kyoto protocol. the european community and all the member states are now legally and politically committed to targets which limit greenhouse gas emissions. we must now take decisions to ensure that we continue to develop our leadership role and deliver on these promises. we politicians all understand that there are costs involved in respecting kyoto. we want these costs to be as low as possible. today's debate is a means to that end. without additional measures, however, the european union as a whole will not meet its obligations under kyoto. indeed, several member states are off-track. in order to fulfil our commitments we need tools both at national and community levels. emissions trading should be one of these tools. if emissions trading is not used, the member states will have to use other policies and measures. the european climate change programme is currently examining measures with stakeholders and emissions trading was among those identified as preferable. we are talking about using a market-oriented instrument for the first time as an eu environment policy instrument. we all appreciate that this is a challenge. with this in mind, the commission proposed a straightforward scheme that was mandatory from the start, concentrated on a limited but considerable number of key actors and which focused on co2, the main greenhouse gas. the big prize before us is the establishment of an eu-wide scheme that will be extensive and will cover approximately half the co2 emissions of the fifteen current member states, candidate countries that will be member states by the time this directive enters into force, and countries of the european economic area. in an era of increasingly integrated markets, the european institutions cannot stand back and let each country develop different national emissions trading schemes. we should all be concerned about the impact on the internal market if different systems were to develop, and the possibility of fragmentation in the evolving internal market in greenhouse gas emission allowances. individual national schemes are not big enough on their own to maximise the economic benefits of emissions trading. therefore we need an emissions trading system which operates across the whole eu. the commission believes that an eu-wide system can save 35% of the costs of complying with the kyoto protocol, or eur 1.3 billion each year by 2010. this is a very considerable cost saving that should be welcomed by everyone, including industry. it is true that in some sectors of industry, there are cheaper cost-reduction potentials than in others. emissions trading uses market forces to ensure that reductions are made where it is cheapest and everyone benefits from these cheaper options. those who make these reductions are rewarded for doing so and those who do not have such cheap options can buy allowances for less than it would cost them to reduce emissions themselves. plant managers, who know the costs better than anyone, should decide whether to go for option one or the other. furthermore, within an eu-wide scheme, the price of an allowance would be the same wherever the plant may be. emissions trading for sulphur and nitrous oxide emissions was so successful in the us that the us continues to develop emissions trading for pollutants other than greenhouse gases. if we can demonstrate that emissions trading can also be applied to greenhouse gases, we will be able to show the us a way in which it may rejoin the international process in limiting greenhouse gas emissions. not only can the eu show them how it is done, but it can also save money at the same time. if emissions trading is a good idea, then it makes sense to start as soon as is practicable. i strongly believe that we should start in 2005, then, by the time the kyoto protocol become legally binding in 2008, we will have gained experience and, if necessary, fine-tuned our use of the instrument. to maximise the cost-effectiveness of emissions trading, a number of preconditions are necessary: first, there must be clear rules; second, clear targets must be set for operators by allocating a fixed number of allowances according to fair and transparent criteria; third, the market should be as large as possible and include both potential sellers and potential buyers; fourth, in order to ensure compliance with the rules a strong framework is necessary. these are the guiding principles upon which we have formulated our proposal and i strongly recommend them to this parliament. finally, i would add that the eu's credibility is at stake. we are being closely watched from all corners of the globe to see whether the eu will live up to its leadership credentials. we need to show that eu is serious and we need to start implementing the necessary measures in order to fulfil our commitments in the first commitment period of the kyoto protocol and beyond.
report drawn up on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy. - mr president, first of all i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr moreira da silva, the other advisory rapporteurs and the shadow rapporteurs for the pleasant way in which we have been able to work together to arrive at the proposal before us. i should like to point out that it has become clear during the process that the proposal on emissions trading is controversial. the difference in views between those in favour and those against led to an overwhelming number of amendments. as rapporteur for the opinion of the economic and monetary committee, i am in favour of a clear and unambiguous system of emission trading, a system in which the rights and obligations of governments and businesses are clearly defined. but it is also a system which respects the very dynamics of the industry, a dynamic in which continuity and scope for competition are not unduly hampered by new rules. it is therefore welcome that the final report now before us incorporates a number of amendments from the economic committee to that end. i am referring in particular to the extension of the time limit in article 11, the adjustment of the penalty system in article 16 and the way in which member states tax the emissions trading system in article 16 (4). the promotion of the proper functioning of a market for allowances has been served by clarity on market-distorting elements. it is therefore regrettable that the environment committee has not been able to reach agreement on the way in which the rights will be allocated from 2008 onwards. it remains of great importance that we remain alert to measures that member states may take to intervene in an emissions trading market through their own regulations and taxes. the resistance to an emissions trading system will persist among various parties and will encourage circumvention of the rules. it is therefore not possible that the lack of clarity in the directive means that emissions trading is doomed to failure. the following are therefore very important in the case of emissions trading: the proof of the pudding is in the eating.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, let me also begin by expressing my thanks. firstly, to the commissioner and her staff. they have put forward a good proposal and have been constantly willing to discuss it with the members of parliament. secondly, to mr moreira da silva, who has tried to improve the proposal with admirable tenacity. and finally to the colleagues in my own group who have had to endure long discussions on this subject. tradable emission allowances proved to be a difficult subject. in all the difficult discussions it has been necessary to remind people from time to time that the objective of all this is kyoto. we must work on the ambition to combat climate change and we must do this in an economically and socially responsible way. in our group, three issues were at the forefront. firstly, we wanted to maintain the environmental integrity of the proposal and strengthen it where possible. we therefore support the proposal by jorge moreira da silva to introduce a cap, an absolute ceiling, so that we can be sure that emissions are indeed going down. we are in principle in favour of cooperation in this field with eastern european countries and developing countries, but in a way which excludes the use of sinks and nuclear energy. secondly, the pse group wants the system we are creating to be fair and to be perceived as just. that is why there must be a credible policy of sanctions, why we absolutely want to avoid disadvantaging early innovators and why the allocation method should be as similar as possible. excessive differences between member states lead to distortions of competition. there are still some differences of opinion, including within our group, on the method of allocation itself - grandfathering or auction. thirdly, the system must be effective. that means the market must be as large as possible: the more players, the more effective! i have to say, the discussion of this was a little alienating at times. i believe that it is not at all attractive for companies to opt out, because these companies have to reduce their co2 emissions anyway. those who do fall within the system can - if they fail to reduce emissions - buy emission allowances on the market. those who are not in the system will have to shut down plants or even parts. in my view, this is not a very social solution. as socialists we take employment into account. companies and trade unions therefore have nothing to gain from an opt-out. perhaps that is why it is a good idea to withdraw amendment no 81. ladies and gentlemen, it is very important that we can report in new delhi on progress in european climate policy. today parliament is taking an important step, next week the council will take the next step. it is also very important that we give the concept of sustainable development a boost after johannesburg. with this report on tradable emission allowances we are doing justice to the environment, but also to economic and social principles. we may disagree on the details, but this is the main line we must keep in mind. today we have the opportunity to choose sustainable development. let us do so with conviction.

in writing. - (nl) financial support for all the countries of eastern europe, where the economy has collapsed in the last ten years and where no major improvement is to be expected in the near future, is absolutely necessary. bosnia and herzegovina is a special case. after the international approval in 1992 of the separation of this former turkish province from yugoslavia, there have been constant attempts from outside to create a state and to obtain the support of the inhabitants to do so. but in fact, it's no man's land. it is a state where only ethnic minorities exist. only the largest minority wanted this country and considers it as the own country of the islamized population during the turkish rule. the other two groups, which felt relegated to the background during the turkish period, now feel closer to the neighbouring states, serbia or croatia. they feel that the present borders are an obstacle and want to remove them as quickly as possible. the count of the last elections is not yet complete, but it is expected that the voters have again opted for the different opposing nationalisms, and that these three groups therefore opt for a separate future. how long do we want to keep this country artificially alive by military force, by externally appointed administrators and by financial means? after this ordeal, our efforts will ultimately fail.

in writing. - (nl) this non-legislative report is full of good things and evidence. more women naturally need to be able to work in knowledge-based sectors such as information and communication technologies. and it seems positive that a 'european worker's statute' is being set up, a european system of labour legislation and social security for mobile workers. this is in line with the questions i am asking the commission today about polish construction workers working without a collective agreement. but the core of the proposal is that it is about adapting people to work, rather than adapting work to people. it provides recipes for how the labour market can be made to work better by focusing education even more on work. its aim is to facilitate the movement of people thousands of kilometres away to a region with another language and culture where there is incidentally more work. if people want to move, it is obviously good that their qualifications are also valid far from home and that they can retain their pension rights. but most people don't want it at all, and rightly so. europe is not america, where people are forced by financial need to move to such places that cut them off from their family and friends. it has to stay that way.
