rapporteur. – mr president, if this debate was scheduled at this time because of the conference of presidents' suspected interest in the subject matter, they were probably right. it is not a very exciting topic to be discussing but, as we all know, it is very important or we would not be here. i have to say it is a shame that two of the three committee members who voted against the report in committee and, therefore, triggered a debate in plenary, are not here today to explain their objections to the report. i would like to thank the committee members who supported me in drawing up this report and giving it near unanimous backing in committee. thanks are due also to the commission for the excellent cooperation we have again had on this report. many of the amendments contained in the committee's report are technical in nature. i am not going to go into that. i just want to mention a few substantive issues the commissioner also raised. the report deals with a number of points where we feel the implementing rules could be strengthened. the first concerns weaknesses regarding the appointment and functioning of senior financial actors, something which has been an issue for the last few months. there have been several instances of transfers or terminations of duties involving directors-general and there has been the case of the accounting officer, mrs andreasson. the issues raised are being dealt with by the committee and assessed on their own merits. however, issues of form have also arisen concerning how such appointments, transfers and terminations are dealt with within the commission. we would like to see certain safeguards built into the financial regulation. safeguards, not in the sense that you can be sure mistakes will never be made or problems will never occur, but safeguards that introduce more transparency to ensure that the process is visible and that we are not faced with surprises and faits accomplis. this involves the appointment of senior officers, something to which you referred, commissioner. i will request that a report be submitted to the budgetary authority and that the accounting officer and internal auditor be appointed on the basis of a vacancy notice in the official journal. they should be external candidates, where necessary on limited-term contracts. i realise that we cannot change the financial regulation but we must take the matter up in the staff regulations, because it is an important point. secondly, there is the question of the financial irregularities panel, which is designed to fill a gap in the existing set-up and introduce new expertise. what we want to avoid is a system where peers are assessing peers. the introduction of an independent external element is, therefore, important, and i welcome the fact that you have accepted that proposal. thirdly, there is the matter of improving the quality and integrity of the computerised accounting system, something you also mentioned. we want a single integrated computer system, with access restricted to a list of authorised persons to be kept by the institution. i realise that the commission is already doing this, and it is important the other institutions should be required to follow. finally, we want to see an easy-to-read audit trail maintained, to ensure adequate control of expenditure. the final point i want to mention is late payments and the need to bring commercial payments in line with the relevant directive. i am sure my colleague, mr casaca, who has worked hard on this, will have something more to say. three amendments have been tabled in plenary in addition to the ones from the committee. one by the ppe-de group and two by the gue/ngl group, none of which i support. the ppe-de is retabling an amendment that was rejected in committee, proposing to create a fully independent accounting officer with no lines of accountability and responsibility within the commission. i cannot support that because it contradicts the financial regulation itself, in relation to which these are implementing rules. nor is there any point in creating an isolated island within the institution, which would go against the whole principle of accountability. great formal power does not necessarily mean better decision-making, as we know. with regard to the amendments by the gue/ngl group, i can agree in spirit with amendment no 34 on the need for the accounting officer to have full information, but in practice it would lead to a huge bureaucracy, with 600 000 payments going through one single person. although not the aim of the amendment, it would certainly lead to unnecessary bureaucracy. the second amendment concerns the proposal on the criteria to be taken into account in the event of a waiver of recovery of an established debt. there are two criteria: one on competition and one on economic and social damage caused by a debt if it is recovered. the gue/ngl group wants to scrap this possibility for authorising officers. the amendment we have introduced and which you have just accepted, introducing a reporting requirement to parliament, offers sufficient safeguards. to conclude, i think these amendments strengthen the proposal and i call on the commission to incorporate them all into the final text.

in writing. - (nl) there was a time when the preparation and implementation of government policy was kept in the greatest possible secrecy, because the ordinary citizen did not have to know what methods and what arguments governed the exercise of power. this cult of secrecy even survived the introduction of universal suffrage. and while today we assume that all individuals are equal before the law, that authorities are accountable to voters, and that information is available about the conduct of public affairs, we are back to traditional secrecy when it comes to public safety, defense, and military matters. this may be justified temporarily, when the majority of the population is threatened by a dangerous minority of profiteers who want to abolish their basic rights. but secrecy can also protect powerful profiteers from popular revenge. the solution chosen - a voluntary agreement between parliament and the council - looks better than it really is. the public opinion has no say in the matter, but parliament does. however, parliament's right of access is limited to a special committee of four members chosen by common accord of the group chairmen and chaired by the chairman of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy. in practice, the vast majority of members of the european parliament - and even whole groups in this parliament - will know nothing. such a committee responsible for security matters therefore only protects secrecy.
in writing. - (nl) medicines are a commercial commodity which makes money. therefore, assessing their use is not a neutral technical issue. competing firms and methods benefit from legislation which allows them to sell their own products as much as possible and to exclude competing products from the market. these companies are aiming to over-consume their product and to exclude parallel medicines. the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection is right to oppose advertising for aids, asthma and diabetes medicines, unlike the commission. the producers and users of alternative medicines, and the doctors who prefer these products, fear that the proposed rules will work mainly to the advantage of the chemical industry and to the detriment of natural products. these are products that may be centuries old, effective according to their users, but whose mode of operation has never been scientifically demonstrated. since they are not harmful and their composition is known, they should be given the benefit of the doubt. it is true that harmful and poor quality products produced for commercial purposes alone must be banned, but there is no reason whatsoever to place the pharmaceutical industry in a monopoly situation. i therefore vote against the industry's proposals and for those advocated by groups of doctors and users.

- mr president, i wholeheartedly agree with the aim of the khanbhai report. the question is how european agriculture can be integrated into the development of agriculture in the third world. i have three comments on this balanced and concrete report. firstly, a proper anti-dumping policy is needed to achieve more reasonable world market prices. the dumping of surplus products on the world market at extremely low prices contributes to the fact that world market prices are often very low. this makes it virtually impossible for farmers in poor countries to participate in world trade on their own on market terms. the european union is still dumping through export subsidies. these subsidies account for 8% of the 40 billion agricultural budget. the abolition of export subsidies should have been more emphasized by the rapporteur. secondly, the situation of poor countries can be improved by greater access to the european market for products which are essential to them. tariff barriers, and in particular non-tariff barriers such as health and environmental requirements, make access to the european market difficult. increasing access is particularly crucial for countries that are active in only one product category, for example bananas, sugar or cotton. the rapporteur recognizes the need for diversification of exports and also makes practical proposals. finally, the trading position of poor countries benefits from targeted development cooperation. the report rightly points to the need for facilitative support. structural aid for basic infrastructure is primarily provided by the member states. the report should therefore leave the decision on the priorities for the use of these funds to the donors and the recipient countries themselves. mr president, on the whole the report contributes to a fruitful relationship between the agricultural sectors of europe and those of the developing countries.

the commission. mr president, i would like to thank you. ladies and gentlemen of the house, you have before you two commission proposals concerning the rotterdam convention on the procedure for the prior approval after information has been given (pic procedure) of certain dangerous chemicals and pesticides in international trade. the decision is to ratify the convention on behalf of the european community and to adopt the regulation necessary to implement it in the community. the decision on ratification hardly needs any further presentation. the commission's proposal for an implementing regulation reflects both the commission's and the member states' view that the provisions should go beyond mere transposition of the convention, which was the result of a compromise between all the parties to the negotiations. the community called for stricter rules in certain respects, but this was not accepted. the commission considers that the proposals are well balanced and will contribute to the achievement of the community's objective of improving the protection of human health and the environment in importing countries, in particular developing countries, from hazardous chemicals, without impeding the smooth application of the convention. the commission is grateful for the support given to the proposals by the committee on the environment. it called on the community to ratify the convention at an early stage, in line with the spirit of the conclusions of the johannesburg summit. the commission therefore hopes that agreement on the implementing regulation, which it considers to be a prerequisite for the continuation of the ratification process, can be reached as soon as possible. in this context, the commission would like to highlight the efforts made by the council and parliament to take the proposals forward, in particular the compromises reached as a basis for a possible agreement between the council and parliament at the first reading of the draft implementing regulation. in conclusion, i should like to thank the rapporteur, mr blokland, and i should have said this first.
the rapporteur. - mr president, it is not often that i get 10 minutes to speak, but i hope i do not need all of them. we have before us, mr president, two reports on the import and export of chemicals. the first report aims to approve the rotterdam convention on certain dangerous chemicals and pesticides in international trade. i suggest that this should be done as soon as possible, since the treaty can enter into force sooner once enough parties have ratified it. the convention focuses on three main points: first, the parties to the convention may only export the chemicals listed in the annex to another party to the convention if they have obtained prior authorization from the importing country. this is called the pic procedure: prior informed consent. secondly, new substances can be added to the annex under the pic procedure. thirdly: in the case of a party exporting prohibited or controlled chemicals, that party shall provide information to the importing party. in addition, all substances listed in the annex which are subject to the pic procedure must be labelled. these matters are more or less already covered by a regulation of 1992. in addition, the chemical industry has already begun voluntary implementation of the rotterdam convention in april this year. there is therefore no longer any reason to wait any longer to ratify the convention. the second report aims at implementing the rotterdam convention by means of a regulation. this regulation goes beyond the rotterdam convention in a number of respects. it has become a little stricter, clearer and broader and this can be seen as an improvement in legislation. the commission is also increasing its efforts to provide information to third countries, especially developing countries. a more difficult point is that in the commission's original proposal, that commission wanted to give itself a monopoly in the procedures. this is not wise, since not all member states have the same legislation on chemicals. i am referring in particular to pesticides and biocides. as you know, it will be five to ten years before we have community legislation on this. moreover, it is possible that member states will continue to use derogation schemes after this period. it is therefore appropriate to leave room for member states in this regulation. the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection has adopted 15 amendments. the legal basis of the regulation has been changed from internal market to environment. this means co-decision for the european parliament. it also creates more freedom for individual member states to take further action. this is reflected, inter alia, in the fact that individual member states may also propose to add new substances to the list for which prior informed consent is required. the fact is that there is still a group of substances for which there is no harmonised european legislation, such as pesticides. another point of improvement is that the lists of dangerous substances should be updated at least annually. it is very important that the persistent organic pollutants have been added to this regulation. the agreements made under the stockholm convention are included in the list of prohibited substances. as it turned out that the council shared the view of the committee on the environment, i, as rapporteur, tried to complete the legislative process in the first reading. i have been given the mandate by the political groups to do this. the negotiations on this subject have proceeded satisfactorily. the council adopted most of the amendments tabled by the committee on the environment. the council's amendments, which were mainly technical, were also well adapted. for this reason 42 new amendments were tabled, which were signed by most of the groups. the council has sent a letter promising that if the european parliament accepts the full compromise package, the council will adopt the common position accordingly. this means that we can conclude the first reading, which is a considerable gain of time of at least a year. i am very pleased to hear from mrs wallström that the european commission is also in full agreement with this. i would like to draw particular attention to amendment no 22. as regards the scope, it was agreed with the council that the rules would in any case apply above a quantity of 10 kg. this will greatly improve the practicability and controllability of the system. this is also part of the overall package. mr president, the compromise package before us is a very satisfactory result which i warmly recommend to parliament. the voting list contains four blocks. block 1 contains the compromise amendments with the council. if block 1 is accepted, block 2 is discontinued. block 3 contains the amendments of the committee on the environment which have been accepted by the council, so we must vote in favour of them. finally, block 4 contains three amendments which must be rejected by parliament in view of the overall compromise. finally, i would like to thank the shadow rapporteurs, the committee on legal affairs and the internal market and the danish presidency for the good and constructive cooperation.
- mr president, trust is a concept that is central to any discussion of economics. our entire economic system is based on trust. and as long as that trust is not betrayed, the economic system functions as we expect it to. expectations in financial markets are closely linked to the way regulatory institutions such as the council, the commission and the parliament deal with unexpected circumstances. the financial markets expect measures, but they expect measures which are clear and do not lend themselves to multiple interpretations. the concept of interpretation in particular plays an important role in the debate on foreknowledge. after all, what is foresight, and when do we speak of foresight that actually has an impact? article 1 of the directive therefore refers to 'substantial influence on the price of financial instruments'. this concept, however, must be interpreted in the light of the practical operation of the directive. it is not possible to set a single rule that applies in every situation. the member states have adopted rules to prevent and punish fraud and insider dealing. the practice shows that in many cases it is a question of an assessment of the facts on the basis of a given situation. it is precisely in the field of practice that i believe the professional group of journalists is able to determine whether there is foreknowledge on the basis of a practical case. in fact, in their daily work they will have to judge whether something is "new" or "foreknown". the purpose for which information is collected or disseminated shall form the basis for assessing whether there is foreknowledge. i shall therefore not support amendments nos 6 and 7. the commission's proposal is to be adopted by the council at the next meeting of the european council in brussels. given that the assessment is based on facts and situations, reference will have to be made to existing rules and self-regulation within the profession. here too, recourse to the professional group is a matter of trust. although i believe that some things should be regulated at member state level, the argument for european uniformity of rules is convincing. in the international context of financial markets, national regulation is lacking. i therefore support the recommendation for the second reading by mr goebbels.

in writing. - the eldr group voted in favour of the lisi report. we have serious reservations about the commission's proposal on compensation for air passengers, however, for the following reasons: 1) the commission proposal has not been subjected to a proper economic impact assessment to determine its potential effect on ticket prices and consumer choice. such an assessment is fundamental to ensure that the proposed system can be sustainable in practice. (2) neither the proposal nor parliament's compromise recognises the fundamental difference between the usual circumstances leading to a refusal of boarding and those leading to a cancellation. while denied boarding is usually the result of intentional overbooking, cancellation is often due to factors beyond the airline's control - air traffic management, for example. the definition of 'force majeure' given by parliament is an insufficient guarantee in this respect. although it can be argued that airlines should, in such cases, turn against the third parties actually responsible, this will be difficult to achieve in practice. 3) the finally, it would be preferable, particularly with regard to low-cost carriers, to require airlines to offer their customers the option of paying an additional insurance premium, which would be added to the ticket price and guarantee them compensation in the event of cancellation or delay beyond the control of the airline.

in writing. - i am in favour of enlargement, but against this resolution, because some points lack a critical approach. first, many candidate countries do not meet the copenhagen criteria. the problems of corruption, arbitrary detention, discrimination and administrative capacity are still too common. secondly, the accession of these new countries is closely linked to a 'big bang' which is due to take place in 2004. it is not the criteria but the date that has become decisive. delaying the accession of a country until it meets the criteria has therefore become politically impossible, while the message is being conveyed that the criteria are not important after all. thirdly, it is acceptable to allow countries to enter even if they do not meet the copenhagen criteria, provided that there are valid review mechanisms (with sanctions) to ensure that these criteria, as well as the acquis, are met as quickly as possible. such mechanisms (which must also apply in the present member states) exist for economic criteria, but not for the rule of law, democracy or human rights. d66 finds these shortcomings even more serious than the economic shortcomings. finally, the reform of the catastrophic agricultural policy is being delayed. the recent agreements between germany and france are totally inadequate. the fact that the old, failed agricultural policy is being introduced first in the new member states only makes a genuine reform in 2007 even more unlikely.

conditions in the host company but also by taking other temporary agency workers as a reference point. so you get something like treating women equally by just comparing them to other women and not to men. secondly, they argue that the directive should be about pay in the first place. we have now received legal opinions from all three institutions that this is indeed possible, since it is a question of comparison and not of determining the level of remuneration. but in doing so, they also try to get the hook out, because pay is, of course, the most important condition of employment. the directive would no longer have any meaning, because then the bulk and, let us say, all of the temporary agency work would fall outside it. i know that in the united kingdom this is also a major in writing. - (nl) when i voted, my main concern was to protect the dutch legislation dating from 1999, which aims to put temporary work on an equal footing with normal work and to protect it from abuse. without such legislation, employers may abuse temporary work to deprive groups of workers of some job security, reduce their pay, reduce their right to participate in decisions, make them work in worse conditions, make early dismissal possible or break strikes of other workers. the aim is to make people permanently dependent by preventing them from obtaining a permanent job with the company that employed them. temporary work is only eligible if it is a deliberate choice, even if the workers remain in the service of a temporary employment agency, and if it is accompanied by all the normal rights for workers. the two main groups have adopted a compromise which is detrimental to the increased protection proposed by my group. however, dutch employers are trying to persuade their colleagues in other member states and the right wing of this parliament to reject even this minimal protection and to have the rules rejected or relaxed. in this way they seek to reduce their costs and increase the number of temporary workers. i can only vote for this report if it prevents these individuals from achieving their aims.

in writing. - (nl) last week the commission put forward radical proposals on quotas. proposals inspired by political feasibility rather than by a justified concern given the poor state of the cod stock. rather than banning cod and minnow fishing, the commission prefers to limit the minimum by-catches of cod by the dutch flatfish fleet. that's what they call putting a plaster on a wooden leg. the management of fish stocks and the quota it gives rise to depend on the accuracy of the catch recording. after a debacle in the 1980s, this recording is now unerringly in the netherlands. 99% of the fish caught is registered and sold via fish auctions. what about the other member states? how can one of the largest member states export twice as much fish as its fishermen take out of the sea, according to the record sheets? the jové peres report rightly calls for increased control and harmonized sanctions. it is high time that this will be put into practice. in the present situation, it is the member states which respect the quota both on paper and in practice that suffer the most.

fresh food and safe food do not always seem to go hand in hand. every year many people die as a result of salmonella and campylobacter poisoning in, for example, chicken. these bacteria can be fought with chemicals, such as the toxic methyl bromide. a major drawback of this method is that some of these toxins remain in the diet. irradiation of food is a good alternative to kill the microorganisms and thus prevent food poisoning. if we want to eat fresh produce, we can't heat it first. to prevent the spoilage of vegetables, fruits and cereals, we can irradiate. so another big advantage of keeping products fresh. however, it cannot be said that this food is irradiated to give it a false "impression" or to mask a defect. any harmful substances already produced by the microorganisms cannot be undone by the radiation. the hygiene and health requirements should therefore continue to apply to the production and agricultural processes. but how do we know that these fresh products are safe? firstly, experience shows that irradiation of food is widely used in countries both inside and outside the european union. moreover, the safety of irradiated food is confirmed by a 50-year history of research by the world health organization and the international atomic energy agency, among others. irradiation of food does result in the formation of new substances, as does cooking food. in the case of fat irradiation alone, it is not entirely clear whether this could have any adverse health effects. this needs further investigation. i conclude from the above that there is a technical need, there is no danger to public health, it is useful for the consumer and that irradiation of food is not an alternative to hygiene requirements. this fulfils the four conditions laid down in the 1999 framework directive. i therefore want to leave room for adding vegetables, fruit and cereals to the positive list. in the committee on the environment, the resolution has been improved by amendment in the right direction. i have one more comment on labelling, however. the labelling must not be such as to constitute a danger or warning sign. if these products have been shown to be safe, a warning is not required. this would only give the wrong impression to the consumer that something is wrong with it. to avoid confusion, it may be sufficient to indicate that this product has been irradiated for hygienic reasons. just as a package of milk states that it has been heated to a certain temperature to kill harmful bacteria. finally, mr president, i conclude that in some cases irradiation of food is necessary to ensure that fresh food and safe food go hand in hand. let us not therefore reject the irradiation of food, but take it upon ourselves.
undine bloch von blottnitz was rapporteur on food irradiation five years ago. then the european commission wanted to move quickly and irradiate much more food than just herbs. first we have discussion, then we have profit. there are different regimes in the 15 countries. in my own country, the netherlands, potatoes are irradiated, but i have never seen that on a label. european law is not being applied properly in these areas. no need for radiation. there are many alternatives. if there were honest labelling, consumers wouldn't buy it. that is why there is fraud in labelling. cyclobutadiene is a substance that is always detectable when food is irradiated. so it's very possible to label it properly because that substance is always detectable. that is the achilles heel of the radiation industry, because consumers don't want it. if it were to be honest, this industry would die a slow death.

the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. the european court of auditors has found that in all years since 1994 and again for the 2001 budget, the books and accounts have been accurate in recording the european union's revenue and expenditure and have also correctly presented the financial situation at the end of the year. at the same time, the european court of auditors has repeatedly asked us to move to a different system for the accounting of assets, one which records financial transactions not only when a payment or receipt has been made but also when a claim has been made or a commitment has been entered into. this is an essential step which is now also laid down in the financial regulation. we have already taken steps in recent years - and i may refer to the question by mr heaton-harris - towards this calculation of assets. however, much of the information about what we have to pay, what we have to do, came from outside the accounting system. let me give you an example. we have asked ourselves what future obligations the commission has in relation to the pensions of its officials. this information was collected and evaluated by the directorate-general for administration and then, as it were, entered into the accounting system. this information has not developed out of the annual budget. i would like to take another example, and that applies to parliament's budget. let's take the fixed assets, let's take this house: the budgetary statement only included the expenditure incurred in a year. if you will, the assets were then no longer included in the accounts, or had to be re-entered with a corresponding valuation. the future is now planned and is being introduced in such a way that information is transferred directly from the annual budget to the asset budget. the european union's assets are then known and do not need to be added separately. i have to point out that unfortunately we cannot simply rely on best practices in the member states either. there are individual member states - and we have repeatedly spoken about this in the committee on budgetary control - which have taken steps in this direction, but at the same time the member states also have different problems. for example, municipalities own infrastructure, so they have different assets and different values to evaluate than we do. if, for example, the collateral that contractors have to provide when they participate in a tender or have been awarded the contract has to be recorded in books, then we have to make new decisions. the international standards are principles, if you will, but they must be made operational in the context of the specific budget, the specific tasks we have, which are broken down, so to speak, in the budget. that will be decided by this standards committee. i believe that if we have good results in this area, perhaps in the future this will be something that member states or third countries can take over from us.

in writing. - (nl) when prices rise, the value of wages decreases. to protect themselves, trade unions have fought for years in many european countries for indexation. this means that compensation for the decline in purchasing power should not be renegotiated every year, but only on the question of how much workers contribute to productivity growth and how to make up the backlog of long-underpaid groups. the pressure exerted by employers' organizations and the support given to them by neoliberal governments have in many cases destroyed this indexation. this may lead to a sharpening of wage conflicts. similarly, there is a renewed attempt to blame the workers for the depreciation of the currency or the lack of money for essential public expenditure. in other words, the right and the bosses believe that the economy will only be good if a majority of the population accepts an insidious decline in purchasing power. they do not take into account the resulting fall in national purchasing power, too high earnings and too low taxes. official statistics on wage costs and price developments are becoming a key data point for wage disputes and for the way governments and employers try to manipulate these disputes. the wage cost indexation regulation will not put an end to this conflict of interest.

in writing. - (nl) because hong kong was once stolen from china and then leased for a time, china was entitled to the return of this territory. this is not without problems for many people who have moved in over time. they enjoy a higher standard of living than the surrounding populations and are more demanding of their administration. while they want to participate in the debate and critical reflection on the actions of public authorities, they are simply transferred from one colonial power to another. while the 'one country, two systems' agreement guarantees the survival of capitalism, it does not guarantee the introduction and development of democracy. that is why it is predictable that many people do not feel safe there and fold luggage. they want to go to europe, america or japan, closer to the kind of society they are used to living in. and the chinese government is determined to make hong kong like the rest of the country. the city can become a showcase but without allowing for prohibited movements or holding normal democratic elections where the opposition could take power. for all these reasons, i doubt that an agreement on the readmission of refugees can work. the idea of making this agreement an example for other states where people with a critical eye do not feel safe is even more open to challenge. i therefore voted against the resolution.

in writing. - (nl) it seems that for some member states enlargement is simply a matter of buying as large a market as possible for their national companies at the lowest possible price. the amounts of the structural funds up to 2006 previously set will therefore have to be distributed among a larger number of new member states than planned. farmers in the new member states will receive much less money than their colleagues in the current member states. the situation could have been worse, but thanks to the compromise proposed by denmark and the pressure exerted on the poles, the copenhagen summit has made it possible to bridge the gap between the rich and the poor. the netherlands, for example, failed to act with calculation. however, there is a strong chance that central europe will remain the poor relative of the west for a long time to come. if a majority of voters opt for eu membership, hoping that they exercise this choice freely and not after a flurry of propaganda, enlargement will take place in 2004 and will probably encompass half of the island of cyprus. the eu must be careful not to get involved in a conflict over the possession of the island and to stay away from pressure to have turkey become a member quickly without having to apply democratic and human rights criteria.
- president, one country, two systems. it almost sounds too good to be true for hong kong. a potential time bomb underneath is at least article 23 of the basic law. this article calls for the development of laws to combat a wide range of serious crimes against the government of the people's republic of china. the hong kong authorities have adopted an opaque implementation of this controversial article at a most unfortunate time. so, at the beginning of this week, hong kong residents came out in droves. does beijing really need to fear treason, secession, insurrection, subversive activities, theft of state secrets or dangerous foreign political activities or connections with hong kong at this time? - no, you won't! nevertheless, the chinese authorities strongly insist on the implementation of article 23. note, an article that only took its current form after the tiananmen square massacre in beijing. article 23 therefore reflects the chinese communist paranoia of then and now. so was the fear of hong kong's citizens then and now. while hong kong, madam president, is going through a difficult economic period, beijing is adding to it a growing political uncertainty. the negative reaction of even the business sector in hong kong speaks volumes here. it reflects a broad civil dissatisfaction with a diffuse consultation process on the legal implementation of article 23. what is missing is the publication of the precise legislative proposals. the council and the commission should address the relevant authorities in hong kong and beijing promptly, since the european union does indeed wish to maintain the principle of 'one country, two systems' for hong kong.
